speakeroldname: Mr. G. D. GRANT (North Ontario) moved:
speechtext:
That a petition for leave to introduce a Bill praying for the incorporation of the Kingston Dominion Central Railway Company be now received, and be referred to the Seleet Stand-inf: Committee on Standing Orders:
He said : Those interested in this Bill had been under the impression that they could utilize the charter granted to them some years ago, but a few days ago they ascertained that they could not do so, and then the time for presenting petitions for private Bills had expired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have not the slightest objection to these petitioners getting relief, but I would point out that the more indulgent the House is the more careless and indifferent become those who seek legislation here. In future any such petitions will have to be founded upon better grounds than those which the hon. member (Mr. Grant) has presented to the House to-day. The mere fact that the gentlemen who are promoting this Bill were under a wrong impression is no reason why the House should be asked to relax its rules.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to draw your attention, and through you the attention of the proper authorities who have charge of the internal economy of this building, to the fact that to-day while I and four or five others were coming down from the Railway Committee in the elevator on the west side of the stairway, a serious accident was only averted by the machinery not giving way too quickly. We got down from the second story to the first story safely enough. After that you would think the elevator was a king's plater out for fast exercise, because it went down to the bottom in a very unnecessary and indecent manner. I do not wish to magnify this occurrence at all, but I wish to draw your attention to it, and to point the moral. Besides a little scare and a severe jolt, nothing occurred of a very serious character ; but the machinery might as well have given way at the top as half way down.

and had it done so, I fancy that some of the first families of this land would he wearing crepe.
Name, name.

However, Mr. Speaker, I think the attention of the government might be called to this point that an elevator is just as much a vehicle for conveying the people as a steamboat or any other public means of conveyance, and that the man in charge of it should know something about machinery, just as the man in charge of the wheel of a steamboat should know something about navigating. I do not wish to magnify the occurrence, but I can assure you that a serious accident might easily happen from people undertaking to run these elevators who are not capable of doing so.

speakeroldname: Hon. JAS. SUTHERLAND (Minister of Public Works).
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend is perfectly right in saying that the man in charge of an elevator should be qualified and that the machine should be the best. I believe our elevators are so, as they are manufactured by the best makers in the country. The matter will be inquired into at once by the chief architect of the department, and if it is found necessary to make any change or improvement, it will certainly be done.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I desire to call attention to an article which appeared in the Toronto [DOT] Globe ' of yesterday reflecting upon me in connection with some observations which I made in this House. The article deals with the country in the province of Ontario through which the Transcontinental Railway will run, and it proceeds :
Mr. Barker, taking pattern from a distinguished provincial leader, speaks of it as ' that Mr. .MACPHERSON.
land of jack pine, poplar and spruce.' This is meant to be depreciatory, although it might be as truthfully said perhaps of the Lake Temis-kaming and Lake St. John regions, in which many hundreds of settlers are making themselves homes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to say that these words did not originate with me. I but repeated the exact words used by the right hon. leader of the government in introducing the resolutions last year. They will be found in Hansard at page 7683. He is referring to a report obtained by the Ontario government through a commission, and the timber of the district is being particularly referred to. I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman used the words with a view to depreciate the country. Probably he did not. But if the Toronto ' Globe ' wants to make an attack on anybody for using the words, I would suggest that it had better attack the right hon. gentleman directly, and not me. The words he used are :
The Timber.
Another point equalled only in importance by the existence of a vast area of agricultural land in this country and its moderate climate is the fact that it is largely covered with extensive forests of spruce, jack pine and poplar.
I think that is the first time these words were heard in this House. The article then goes on :
Against such statements we have the observations of men who explored the country with the special view to forming an opinion as to its value.
Why, these are the very observations quoted by the right hon. gentleman from the persons who were appointed by the Ontario government to explore the country and report upon its merits. Under these circumstances the ' Globe ' is somewhat off the track, and the next time it wants to attack any person for using these particular words, it had better make its attack on the right hon. gentleman.
This matter does not concern me, but if I am to understand by what the hon. gentleman has said that he is not only quoting my words but taking their spirit, I have no fault to find at all.

speakerposition: topic
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I wish to again draw the attention of the Postmaster General to the mail service we are receiving from the west. Yesterday the new time table for the Grand Trunk Railway went into force and I saw no change with reference to either the passenger or mail train. The mails from the west arrive at Brockville twenty minutes after the Canadian Pacific Railway train leaves for Ottawa, so that we are still only receiving one mail a day from all the trains east of

Toronto on the Grand Trunk Railway. Two weeks ago I drew the attention of the Postmaster General to this matter and he intimated that before the new time table came into force some change would be made, but so far there has been none.

The hon. gentleman did a couple of weeks ago state that the mails for Ottawa failed to make connection at Brockville, because the Canadian Pacific Railway left a few minutes before the 2.40 Grand Trunk Railway train arrived from the west.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is the passenger train, the mail train comes later. The fast train passes the mail train at Kingston. If the hon. gentleman could have it so arranged that the mail train would deliver the mails to the first train at Kingston for Brockville, that might meet the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I have discussed the matter with the controller of the mail service and expressed the hope that it might be possible to arrange the question, and he is endeavouring to do so. The hon. gentleman asks to have some change made with reference to the limited express. That is where the difficulty offers. Of course, the difficulty could be got over if the Canadian Pacific Railway would make connection at Brockville. I have asked them to make connections but they have not answered although my communication was sent them nearly two weeks ago. I do not think there is any provision in the law whereby we can compel railways to make closer connections and I have no objection to the question being brought up frequently, because I think the time has arrived when our laws should be amended so as to give us more control.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The mail train last year arrived at Brockville ahead of the limited. This year it only arrives at Kingston ahead of the limited. There should be no difficulty in having the train start twenty to thirty minutes earlier from Toronto.

In the Bill as printed, the schedule showing the agreement is dated the 18th of February and the motion of the right hon. gentleman refers to a contract of the 7th of March. The contract was actually signed on the 7th of March.

speechtext: That is not the date of the agreement; that is an error.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
In that case the motion of the right hon. the leader of the government was not correct, because it is a motion to introduce an agreement dated 8th of March.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a clerical error. The agreement produced in connection with the motion is dated 18th of February.
As a matter of fact, it has two dates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The date of the agreement is that which is set forth in the beginning. In some reports the date of the agreement is construed as that on which it is executed. Either one or the other must be the true date.
On Section-9 of the schedule,
9. Notwithstanding anything in the twenty-seventh paragraph of the said contract contained, the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall not, after the acquisition of the twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) of common stock therein mentioned (less shares held by directors, not exceeding one thousand), be prevented from making any such disposition of such common stock as the said Grand Trunk Railway may deem expedient, provided, however, that the said Grand Trunk Railway Company shall, during the delay mentioned in the said paragraph, continue to hold a majority of the said stock by such title as shall enable the said Grand Trunk Railway Company to control the policy of the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
By section 4 of the Act to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific it is provided that the capital stock shall be $45,000,000. Section 5 provides that this stock may be divided into preference and ordinary stock, namely $20,000,000 preference and $25,000,000 ordinary. Subsection 2 of the same paragraph is as follows :
Holders of such preference stock shall be shareholders within the meaning of this Act, and shall in all respects possess the rights and be subject to the liabilities of shareholders within the meaning of this Act ; provided, however, that in respect of dividends and otherwise, they shall, as against the ordinary shareholders. be entitled to the preference and rights given by such resolution.
Section 27 of the original agreement provides :
The company undertakes that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall acquire and take the common stock to the amount of $25,000,000, except shares held by directors, not exceeding 1,000 shares, and shall hold the same during the term of the said lease, and so long as any of the bonds guaranteed by the government under the terms of this agreement shall remain outstanding unpaid.
By the legislation introduced for the purpose of giving effect to that agreement, chapter 71 of the statutes of last session, it was provided by clause 7, subsection 2 :

2 Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the agreement contained, His Majesty the King, acting in respect of the Dominion of Canada, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, undertakings, conditions or stipulations in the agreement contained on behalf of His Majesty, acting as aforesaid, unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada covenants and agrees as follows with His Majesty, acting as aforesaid :-
Subclause (a) which follows, is not material to the present agreement. Then subclause (b) :
(b.) That it will acquire and take the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the amount of not less than $24,000,000, as in clause 27 of the agreement 'provided.
And here is an important subsection of section 7.:
3. The Grand Trunk Railway; Company of Canada shall hold the said common stock to the amount aforesaid so acquired and taken as aforesaid during the entire term of the lease mentioned in clause 20 of the agreement, and so long as any of the bonds guaranteed by the government under the terms of the agreement remain outstanding and unpaid : and no pledge, transfer or conveyance of any part of the said' stock during the said period shall be valid or effectual.
Thus, it is provided not only that they shall take the $24,000,000 of common stock, but that they shall hold that common stock (luring the period of the lease. That is to say for fifty years, and so long as any of the bonds guaranteed by the government remain outstanding and unpaid, they shall hold that stock and shall not be permitted to pledge, transfer or convey any part of it. The purpose of the amendment is to provide that, having taken this common stock-and there is no change with regard to that; they have to take the same amount of stock-they shall not be obliged to hold it ; but they may pledge, transfer or convey it, provided that they hold a sufficient amount to enable them to control the policy of the company. In order to do that, it is necessary that they should control the majority of the $45,000,000 of stock-say somewhere in the neighbourhood of $23,000,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I maintain tliat we are not at all concerned as to what these two companies do in reference to that. If it were stock that was to be placed on the market and sold, I could at once recognize that we would have a great deal of interest in it.
The government thus spoke through the Minister of Finance. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) sat there and listened and did not dissent. The Minister of Justice and all the members of the government listened to this. Do they not recognize that between October and February, they have absolutely turned their faces in the opposite direction and are now doing that which in the month of February, 1903, they said was against the public interest V The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) did not stop there, he went on further :
If this stock were to be put upon the market and taken over by the Grand Trunk Railway Company-I will take the figures of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition for illustration-at 25 cents on the dollar, and in latef years it passed into the hands of other people at 100 cents on the dollar, if the question of freight rates comes to be adjusted at any time, and it becomes a question whether we are to have such freight rales as will earn a fair dividend on the 100 cents that the present holder paid or on the 25 cents that originally went into the treasury, there certainly is much to be said in favour of the man who purchased the stock and who says : ' I paid 100 cents on the dollar for it.'
The government are at the present time putting it in the power of the Grand Trunk to accomplish that which was thus denounced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). They are permitting the Grand Trunk to speculate in this stock ; last year they said it would be against the public interest to do so, last year they said it would Li wrong to do so ; last year they could not permit a measure of this kind, and within four months they have changed their minds upon this question absolutely, and they do the very thing they denounced last year, the very thing which, according to the statement of more than one of them was not to be permitted and could not be, permitted owing to the safeguards which were contained in the agreement as it was originally entered into. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) went on further and said at page 11231 of ' Hansard ' :
I think that the strength of this enterprise is to be found in the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are not only behind it, hut that they are in it and of it. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company take over this new stock at 25 cents on the dollar, they cannot sell it to anybody at 26 cents on the dollar the next day, and they cannot sell it later on for 100 cents on the dollar. It must stay in the treasury of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Well, what is the position now ? It is absolutely the one which the Minister of Finance said could not be accomplished under the agreement of last year, and Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
which in fact could not he accomplished under that agreement, and one which he said last year was absolutely prejudicial and injurious to the public interest.
Further on he said at page 11851 :
The stock will not he allowed to go into the market and pass into the hands of other persons, and possibly at a later stage, be treated in the fixing of the freight rates, as capital at a fictitious value.
Well, why does the government, taking that stand they did in October, 1903, permit this stock to go into the stock market, to pass into the hands of other persons and at a later stage to be treated in fixing freight rates as capital at a fictitious value. What does the Grand Trunk give for the stock? Nothing but the two undertakings which I have mentioned. Yet, that stock, under the terms of this agreement, can he placed on the market and sold by tlie Grand Trunk Company for a very considerable sum, and afterwards that stock will come forward and will have to be considered in the fixing the freight rates as capital for which the holders may possibly have paid 100 cents on the dollar. The Minister of Finance did not stop there. He said :
We think it important, for several reasons, that the Grand Trunk should take and hold that stock and not dispose of it. Instead of that being merely a privilege given to the Grand Trunk Company, we think it is a privilege which carries certain responsibilities of value to the country. Therefore we insist that they shall acquire, take and hold that stock.
Could anything. I ask the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), be more significant and more decisive than that ?
We think it important, for several reasons, that the Grand Trunk should take and hold that stock.
If it 'was important that, the Grand Trunk should take and bold that stock In October, 1903. when did it cease to be important that the Grand Trunk should bold that stock and for what reasons did it cease to be important that the Grand Trunk should hold that stock ? What are the compelling reasons which influenced the mind of the government in this regard ? The Minister of Finance says :
We think it important, for several reasons.
What were those reasons and when did they cease to have cogency and how is it that they ceased to be cogent within so short a period as that between October, 1903, and February, 1904?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said :
Therefore, we insist that they shall acquire, take and hold that stock.
If the government for these good reasons insisted that the Grand Trunk should acquire, take and hold the stock in October, 1903. there must have been some very extremely strong influences wbicli operated

upon the mind of the government between October, 1903, and February, 1904.	.
But the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has not thrown any light upon that subject. He went still further. He said, at page 11850 of ' Hansard ' :
We claim that we do get from the old Grand Trunk Company two things of importance to which I have referred-one that they should take and hold the stock and thus identify themselves closely with the undertaking, and the second that they should become the guarantors of the bonds to the extent of one-quarter or possibly more of the balance required for the building of the western division. In these two things we have obligations on the part of the Grand Trunk which we think are of value ; and, if additional obligations on the part of the old Grand Trunk Company are asked, as in the amendment of my hon. friend, all we can say is that they are not in the contract, and we have no right to demand them.
He said in that extract:
We claim that we do get from the old Grand Trunk Company two things of importance.
The two things of importance were, first, a guarantee of the bonds, and secondly that they shall take and hold the stock, or rather, that which I have put last, the hon. Minister of Finance put first. He regarded as all important two things, and the one which he put first was that the old company should hold the stock and thus identify itself closely with the undertaking. But something even more significant than all this was said by the hon. Minister of Finance : The Grand Trunk Company would be delighted to have that clause stricken out, so that they might be allowed to take that stock up and float it in the money market if they pleased. no doubt.
Since the hon. Minister of Finance was not willing to give them that privilege at that time, for what reason and by what influence has the government been induced to depart from that strong, firm stand which the hon. Minister of Finance then took ?
The Grand Trunk Company would be delighted to have that clause stricken out.
Well, the Grand Trunk Company have accomplished their end, because virtually they have that clause stricken out. They have that clause stricken out, at least, as far as 812,000,000 of the stock is concerned, which is a very considerable instalment of the delight to which my hon. friend referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would my hon. friend allow me to interrupt him ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The capital stock of the company is fixed tit $45,000,000. which may be divided into $20,000,000 of preference shares and $25,000,000 of ordinary stock. By subsection 2 of clause 5 the preference shareholders are absolutely in the same position in respect to electing the directors and
controlling the policy of the company as the ordinary shareholders. Therefore, if we are to give effect to these amendments ; if the men who hold the stock desire to control the policy of the company, they must control the majority of $45,000,000 of shares.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not see how that affects the point I am making.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend said that they were obliged to take and hold $12,000,000 of stock.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, I was putting the case as strongly as I could from the standpoint of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, so that I should not be accused of exaggerating. I said that at least this clause gives to the Grand Trunk Railway Company the right to place on the stock market and to speculate in $12,000,000 of the common stock of this company. I think moreover it gives them the right to put upon the stock market and speculate in the whole of the common stock which they acquire from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. I think it does that under the concluding provision that I (iave mentioned and which I will mention again. By means of what is called a voting trust, which is a well-known institution in the United States of America, I believe that can be done. There are very significant words in the agreement which point irresistibly to the conclusion that the draughtsman who framed that paragraph had in view that verv scheme when he used certain words which are at the end of this clause. But,
I was referring, when interrupted by the hon. Minister of Justice, to the emphatic language of the hon. Minister of Finance.
I was then reading his statement as follows:
The Grand Trunk Company would be delighted to have that clause stricken out, so that they might be allowed to take that stock up and float it in the money market if they pleased, no doubt.
I challenge the hon. Minister of Justice or any one on the other side of the House to say that this clause dues not, at least, give to the Grand Trunk Railway Company the power to float $12,000,000 of the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company on the stock market, and I point out to him in that connection what the hon. Minister of Finance said further. Following on immediately after the language which I have quoted the hon. Minister of Finance said this :
That, I have no doubt, would be more gratifying to the promoters of (his enterprise.
The government had insisted that there should be no speculation in this stock. The government had declared that stock should not be acquired by promoters for a nominal consideration and afterwards go into the hands of bona fide holders and be

used for the purpose of increasing [DOT] the rates upon this railway, in order that dividends might be paid upon stock for which no consideration was given in the first instance. The hon. Minister of Finance insisted that such a result should not take place. He said very frankly that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would like to have all safeguards' of that kind stricken out, and that to strike them out would be highly gratifying to the promoters of the enterprise ; yet, while we were hearing the very echo of these words, in the short interval between the 24th October and the 18th February, the government came to an exactly opposite conclusion. The government acted upon an absolutely different policy to that which the hon. Minister of Finance had proclaimed in this House, and the government did the the very thing which, according to the view that the hon. gentleman then entertained, and according to the view which I think most people In this country will entertain, will be injurious to the public interest in the future, because it will not only permit speculation in stock, but it will result in higher rates being imposed upon the people of this country by reason of the fact that stock which does not represent any real money consideration put into the enterprise will have to be treated as worth par, will have to be dealt with in the hands of men who have paid one hundred cents on the dollar for it. and in that way will very materially influence rates. The hon. Minister of Finance went on farther and emphasized the same point. He said :
We have put that limitation in, not to please the Grand Trunk Company but as an additional guarantee to the people that the stock is not going to be placed in the market and floated at a fictitious value.
Is there any answer at all in the mouth of my hon. friend the Minister of .Justice to the argument which I am quoting against him from the mouth of his own colleague, expressed only a few months ago? But, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance did not even stop there. He said:
1 say, unhesitatingly, that it would be better to give it to the Grand Trunk, even without any other condition, than it would be to have i- dealt out to be used by stock speculators m the market.
Most emphatic, most vigorous language; yet. the very evil against which, according to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, under the agreement of last year, the country was thoroughly safe-guarded, is now permitted by the amended agreement executed only a few months after these very words were uttered. Yet. my hon. friend did not stop there. He went on further: But we are protecting the people against any such condition, because we are refusing the company the power to put a dollar's worth of that stock on the market and sell it to any Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
one. It is not negotiable, it cannot go on the stock market, it cannot be the subject of speculation ; no innocent third party will be able to come and say : ' I paid in good faith 100 cents on the dollar for that stock and am entitled to get a dividend on what I paid. We have stipulated that the stock cannot be put on the market. It must remain in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railwray during the term of this lease.
It is absolutely inconceivable, Mr. Chairman, that after the government had taken such a stand upon this question, after the government had declared so firm a policy during the past session, after this extraordinary clear, vigourous and determined language had been used by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, the hon. Minister of Justice should rise in his place as if this were a very ordinary provision, as if this were a matter of course, and ask this House and the country to accept a clause which wipes out every one of the safeguards to which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance referred in the passages that I have quoted, and which . exposes this country to all the difficulties and dangers that were pointed out in the quotations that I have made. It can not be any ordinary influence that induced the government to change its policy in this way ; there must be some extraordinary reason for it which has not yet been disclosed to the House. What is it ? There is plain language which points to these evils, with all the vigour, and all the clearness and all the energy which are the attributes of the Finance Minister, and he spoke for the colleagues that sat around him. Why are we asked to-day to accept an amendment which absolutely stultifies every word uttered by the Finance Minister last session ? I brought this matter to the attention of the House when the Prime Minister introduced the resolutions, but no answer has been made, and no explanation has been given of this extraordinary change of attitude. The Minister of Justice merely dealt with the legal aspect of the change, but he never uttered a word of explanation as to why be should ask parliament and the country to be satisfied with this complete reversal of the government's policy. When the Prime Minister introduced this measure, he said the changes were so simple and moderate, that we on this side of the House might be expected to accept them without discussion. Does he regard as an unimportant thing, which we should accept without discussion, a complete reversal of the declared policy of his government on a question of very great public concern. I could give quotation after quotation; I could quote from the Minister of Justice and other members of the cabinet, but I shall refrain, because tbe language of the Finance Minister may be taken as a sample, and I now most respectfully ask : why it is that the policy of the government has been reversed so suddenly and so unexpectedly, and why it is

that we now have parliament asked to com- I mit itself to an exactly opposite policy to that which was proclaimed by the government last session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is exceedingly grati-tying to me to find that even at this late date the hon. the leader of the oposition, has such intense admiration for my speech of last session. It enables me to indulge in the hope that I shall have only to wait for a year, when the hon. gentleman will discover that what I say now is couched in wise and discreet language.
What about last night '!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Last night, I had a difference with my hon. friend from Hamilton ; he was right and I was wrong, and I said so, and that was the shortest way of dealing with it. I do not understand that the hon. leader of the opposition takes any ' exception to the opinions I expressed last session when dealing with that document which has since been changed. Why my hon. friend should labour at such great length to show that something which I said last session respecting the contract of that day, does not apply to the contract of the present day, I do not quite clearly understand. There is a change and if there were no change we should have no need of legislation to-day ; and we should have no need of discussing the question. What was the situation last year ? My hon. friends opposite had contended in their press, and by the general tenor of their speeches, and by the general trend of their whole criticism, that this railway scheme was a scheme of promoters who were to put stock on the market for speculative purposes. That was the general line of theii; argument in parliament and in the press. It was in answer to criticisms of that character that I drew attention to the provision of the contract in the clause which the hon. gentleman has read, and I indulged in the comments which he has quoted. Quite so ; I thought it necessary. I think it would have been better if we had been able to continue with the contract of last year. I think we made a great contract last year. And, although hon. gentlemen opposite decried it and stated that it was quite evident that the Grand Trunk Company had their own way, I think the contract of last year was by all odds the best railway contract that ever was submitted to the parliament of Canada. If we were coming forward to-day with this contract in its present form for the first time, we would still surprise hon. gentlemen opposite by the moderation of the contract, and by the many guards and checks which are provided for the protection of the public interest. If there is criticism of these amendments to-day, it is simply because the contract of last year was surrounded to a greater extent than ever before, by the guards and checks which it was thought necessary to insert in the public interest. The hon. the leader of the opposition now says : Why the change ? It is simply and solely because the Grand Trunk Company refuse to go on under the contract of last year. There is no other reason. What other reason could there be ? The Grand Trunk people have come to the government and have said :
* In a variety of ways you have made this contract too hard.' Perhaps we have some reason to complain of the Grand Trunk people ; but not with respect to their good faith, because we have no doubt that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays and all these gentlemen (although they have been decried by an hon. gentleman opposite as fakirs) acted in good faith. When Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays and all their associates in the contract entered into this agreement and gave us the assurance of the co-operation of the Grand Trunk Company, we had reasonable grounds for believing that the company would co-operate in the maner indicated, but we were well aware that the Grand Trunk Company by its meeting of shareholders would have to ratify

that agreement; we were well aware that it had to pass that ordeal.
By and by the Grand Trunk people came to us and said : 1 We cannot go on ; you have tied us up too strictly ; you have made your contract so good for the government that we are not prepared to go on with it, and you must consider one of two things-either to throw up the transaction, or to consider with us the various amendments which we desire.' And the government, wisely or unwisely it is for parliament to judge, decided that a great scheme of this character should Dot be put in peril by matters which might seem to be of small detail; and therefore they agreed to enter into negotiations with the Grand Trunk people and see if they could make concessions which would meet their wishes and yet leave the public interest reasonably protected. X say at once that it would have been better if we could have held to the contract of last year, as respects this particular section, though I do not admit that the change we make creates the danger suggested by my hon. friend. Now, what was the position last year ? We had provided that the Grand Trunk Bailway Company should take and hold this $25,000,000 of common stock ; and when hon. gentlemen opposite alleged that this was to be a speculative stock, we pointed out, as the hon. gentleman has quoted, that it could not be the subject of speculation, because by the terms of the contract the Grand Trunk Company were obliged to take it and hold it, and could not put it on the market. That was an absolutely correct interpretation of the contract as it stood. What is the situation to-day ? The Grand Trunk people say they require to use that stock, or some portion of it, in order to raise money for the purposes of the enterprise. They say to us : You claim that you wanted the Grand Trunk Company to be in and of this scheme ; you wished to keep the Grand Trunk Company in control, so that the new I'oad should be identified as closely as possible with the old. And we have agreed that the Grand Trunk Company, while at liberty to pledge this stock to raise money on it, must still hold a sufficient title to the majority of the stock to control the affairs of the new company. That was one of the main purposes of the clause in the former contract. That purpose is still subserved by the amended clause, because we still provide that while the Grand Trunk Company shall be the holder of the stock, and shall have the right to pledge it for the purpose of raising money, it shall still be bound to hold a controlling title in the majority of the stock. Now, the chief objection that is raised to the overcapitalization of railways to what may be called the watering of stock, is the relation that stock may bear to the important question of freight rates. I pointed that out in my remarks of Iasi year, which have been quoted by the hon. leader of the opposition. I said that if

this stock went on the market and became the subject of speculation, the holders of it might at a later stage come in and say that in the adjustment of freight rates they should be considered as having paid full value for that stock, even though a smaller value had in reality been paid. That was the substance of the argument. It would be always better if we could prevent a com pany raising questions of that character. For that reason, it would have been better if we could have held by the contract of last year. But, as the Grand Trunk Company said they could not go on upon these terms, it was for the government to consider whether the amendments were of such a character as could be agreed to. Why is it that this question of the capitalization of a railway is looked on with some sensitiveness and anxiety by the public in connection with the question of freight rates ? It is because the country has had an experience- shall I say an unhappy experience ?-'by the contract made by the former government with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It is because that contract contains a clause providing that until a certain rate of interest is earned on the capital the freight rates shall not be reduced. It became important, then, to know what was the stock on which interest had to be earned. Unfortunately, the former government either overlooked that point, or did not have their attention drawn to it; and in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract we have no clear definition of what is to be deemed the stock on which the company must earn 10 per cent before there can be any control of its freight rates. Some of these days I suppose that question may have to be determined in the courts. In the light of that experience it is desirable that we should guard against a repetition of the danger. If we had in this contract any 10 per cent clause, then the change which we are making in the agreement on this point would be a vital and important one. But I want to call the attention of the committee to the fact that there is no 10 per cent clause in this agreement. While in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway the right of parliament to revise the freight rates is limited and restricted by the terms of the contract, there is no limit or restriction in this contract as to the right of the parliament of Canada to exercise the fullest and most complete control over the freight rates -of this new enterprise. The consequence will be that the freight rates, in the terms of the contract, will be fixed by the government of Canada, or by any tribunal which parliament may create for that purpose. Parliament has since created a tribunal. that is, the Railway Commission. Parliament may at any time repeal the Act creating the Railway Commission, and may devise some other means of asserting parlia mentary control : but. be it noted, that there is no limit to the control of parliament over the rates of this new enterprise. Let us see

what will happen when the question of rates comes to be considered. Suppose the Grand Trunk people come forward and say : We ask you to allow us to earn interest on this common stock. If we had the contract as it was last year, we would have an extra guard and check, I admit. We are changing the contract in that respect, giving up one guard and check winch we had last year. But let us see what sort of guard we shall still have. When the Grand Trunk people conie before the Railway Commission or before any other tribunal which parliament may create to deal with the question of freight rates, the tribunal will have the full and unlimited right of determining the freight rates, and investigating the circumstances under which every dollar of the capital may have been floated ; and, therefore, if that capital be the subject of specu Iation. in such a manner as to claim dividends on stock which is not bona fide, which never entered into the road, we have no 10 per cent clause limiting us, as in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; but we have the most full and absolute right in a tribunal created by the parliament of Canada to investigate that matter and to see that freight rates are only fixed with reference to the capital bona fide invested in the enterprise. I think that is a fair answer to my hon. friend. We have undoubtedly made a change in this contract which gives. the Grand Trunk Company liberty to deal with this stock in a way in which they had not a right to deal with it a year ago, limited no doubt by the controlling power they must retain. They may pledge the stock for raising money, and to a certain extent there may be an element of speculation in it ; and we have given up some of the guards and cheeks which we had in the contract of a year ago. But we had to consider the question, in respect to that and several other matters, whether these changes were vital and important enough to induce the government to give up the whole enterprise. The conclusion of the government was that, while the contract would be in a less desirable form than it was a year ago, it was still a good contract, free from evils which could be found in other contracts, and that in this particular matter of freight rates the government had amply and adequately protected the interests of the public by inserting in the contract a clause which is not in any degree modified, namely, that the freight rates must, without any limitation, be subject at all times to the control of a body created by the parliament of Canada.

I am prepared to listen to an argument on that point, but as a commercial, venture it cannot be defended-It cannot be defended as a means of keeping Canadian trade within Canadian channels. If the Prime Minister and his colleagues would this session propose a measure to improve our Canadian waterways, so-that they may compete with the improved American water-ways, then they would propose a policy of great national importance. But, if we stand idle and rely upon this Grand Trunk Pacific to carry western trade to our maritime provinces, not only will we lose our money, but we will lose our trade, and waste time into the bargain. I am r ot speaking from a sectional standpoint ; I have studied the question carefully and conscientiously, and I know that the only way to compete with our neighbours to the south is to take a leaf out of their book, and improve our water-ways, while we are improving our railways. The geography of the country is in our favour ; the city of Quebec and the chief cities of the maritime provinces will always get more trade by water than by rail. The St. Lawrence is a natural trade route ; the Americans know it, and that is why they are making such strenuous efforts to improve. their waterways. We are a young nation ; we ere not as powerful as they ; but we are growing bigger, and we understand our 1 osition better now than ever before. I again impress upon the Prime Minister that freight rates can never be controlled by this transcontinental national railway. It is impossible to make that northern road a commercial route. Our' friends from the Northwest know as well as we do, that they must continue to use the great lakes as an outlet for their products, and they know very well also that they will use Canadian or American outlets, just depending on which Is the cheaper. The Grand Trunk may tomorrow build a road between Duluth and Winnipeg, or they may enter into an arrangement with Mr. Hill, and if the rates under this arrangemtent are cheaper than the rotes by the Canadian route, the Canadian [DOT][DOT]oute will lose the trade. There is no pos-

sible doubt about that. I do not find fault with the Grand Trunk ; their geographical position gives them the preponderance of interest in the United States ; and Canada has helped them to locate their line tin it is at present located. Confederation was not accomplished then, and we were not a united nation. But, we are a united nation to day. Let me tell my right hon. friend, that I never understood him ; 1 cannot understand him now when he says, that his main object in this Bill is to give the control of the enterprise to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I cannot make out what he means by that. The Grand Tiunk Company is a great company, and an energetic company controlled by energetic men. When we have all passed away, the Grand Trunk will have to look to how it can best earn money. I hope I am mistaken in the prophecy, that to serve their -own interests they will have to give much of that Canadian western trade to their American connections. On the other hand, if we improve our water-ways, and encourage our railways leading to the Georgian Bay and to the St. Lawrence, we may expect that the Grand Trunk Company will send a great deal of traffic to Canadian seaports. With that object in view, a couple of years before I left office, I placed before the Prime Minister a public document-not a private document-in which I suggested, amongst *other things, that the Montreal harbour <lebt should be assumed by the federal government, and that the port of Montreal should be equipped to handle the trade that is in store for it. If we had more ele ' ators in Montreal, and if we had elevators at Levis and Quebec then in the fall months the steamers carrying grain would do for our Canadian ports, what such steamers are doing for American ports.' Grain would be accumulated, and the Intercolonial Railway and the new railway, if it is ever built, would have so much more trade to carry in the winter months. Let us not forget that we have about seven months of summer trade, during which the railways cannot possibly compete with the waterways1. What business man will say that a cargo of grain will leave Brandon or Winnipeg in the sum iner months, and be carried to Quebec oi to our maritime ports by an all-rail route.
'1 liat will never be done ; in summer the grain will go by water and by rail and water. This Transcontinental Railway will start from Winnipeg, and go to Quebec and Moncton, through a country which is not settled.
I hope the land through which it runs will be found of good quality-as to that we have now no evidence-and if the land is of good quality, the country will be settled in the course of time. But for many years to come there will be no local trade available for that railway. How many millions of bushels of grain will be taken all-rail in the winter months ? Well, at the present day, neither the American nor the Canadian
railways carry any considerable quantity of grain in the winter months1 for export, because it cannot be done on a paying basis.
I cannot insist too strongly on this point, that that route cannot possibly be a commercial route to carry through trade from the west to the east and from the east to the west. We have, then, only one thing to do. If we do not want the Grand Trunk to carry all the Canadian trade from the west to American ports, we have to improve our water-ways in such a way as to induce the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern, and even the great American railroads, to direct their trade to our route because it will be the cheapest. Mr. Chairman, I have not taken part in the discussion on this question so far; but I wanted to lay my views before the House to the best of my ability with the main object that we have all at heart-to keep our trade within Canadian borders, and how to divert traffic from the American centres of trade to our route, which we can do, because it is the shortest. From the head of Lake Superior to Liverpool the Canadian route is about 600 miles shorter than the American route. Let us improve our water-ways, but let us not of course forget our railways. If we improve our water-ways so as to make them co-operate with our system of railways, we shall certainly keep our trade and improve our position. But if we rely on this project to keep our trade, we shall certainly not succeed. Mr. Chairman, I apologize for having said so much.

Mr. Chairman, as I have not taken part in this debate up to the present time, I would like to say a few words in reply to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) who has just taken his seat. The facts which he has presented are not new. He has in season and out of season advocated the water-ways against the rail route. But I am afraid that his conclusion is not right, for the simple reason that he has not taken into account the fact that the grain crop of the Northwest does not mature until late, and it is late when we get our threshing done. Before it is ready to ship navigation is closed, and it is necessary for our farmers to store their grain for six months at the head of the lakes. Now, I want to inform the hon. gentleman, if he does not know it, that it costs six cents a bushel, if not more, to store that grain at the head of the lakes.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ? How many millions of bushels of grain were stored last winter ?

It dees not matter how much was stored last winter. There have been millions of bushels stored there during the winter; and if we believe in the great development of that country that is going to take place, we must believe that in the

near future it will produce several hundreds of millions of bushels of grain every season. Under the best conditions, it is not possible to get more than half the grain crop out of the Northwest during the season of navigation. The balance would have to be stored at the head of the lakes for six months, at a cost of six cents or seven cents a bushel to the producers. Moreover, this would prevent them getting the benefit of any possible rise in the market, that might'occur during the winter. Then, it is not only the grain trade of the Northwest that we have to look to. We have a vast area of grazing lands in that country, and our cattle trade is going to assume enormous proportions in the future. That trade will not be carried over the canals. It must also be remembered that the population of the Northwest is increasing by leaps and bounds, and in a short time will be very large. Does the hon. gentleman suppose that those people are going to do business only six months in the year V Does he suppose that they are going to wait until the ice gets out of the canals every season before doing business ? As a matter of fact the supplies for that country go in during the winter months. If a merchant waited till navigation opened, by that time the spring trade would be over. We in the west expect to consume goods made by the eastern manufacturers in Quebec and Ontario, and these goods will come in during the winter months. If we could get the grain out during the season of navigation, thei-e might be something in the argument of the hon. gentleman ; but he knows that that is not the case. With regard to his statement about the Grand Trunk being able to get a short collection with Duluth, I fancy Uie hon. gentleman is aware that the Canadian Pacific Railway now has a line to Duluth. I do not know what position the, hon. gentleman occupies. I do not know whether he is supporting the proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition or not. If he is, his argument was not very logical, because he says that the Grand Trunk people pay 3 per cent on their bonds. Where .are they going to get the money to do that if the trade is taken from them ? It appears to me that if the proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition were carried into effect, and the government were going to build a road such as he proposes, we would have to spend a lot of money to operate that road. We would be taking more chances than we are doing now, because we have the Grand Trunk Railway Company behind this proposition, and they are obliged to pay 3 per cent on the cost of the road ; whereas, if it were a government road, we would not know, with the object lesson of the Intercolonial Railway before us, whether we eould operate it at a profit or not. What is the proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition ? Last year he proposed

and I do not suppose he has changed his mind since-to cut a big piece out. of the Canadian Pacific Railway system. W hat would that mean ? Where would the whole of the trade go which the Canadian Pacific Railway now brings from China and Japan ? Would it go through Canadian channels ? I think my hon. friend will agree that if you took a piece out of the middle of the Canadian Pacific Railway system, that trade would go by the Canadian Pacific Railway Soo line to Duluth and find an outlet through the United States. I fancy the proposition of the bon. leader of the opposition would have that effect. The hon. gentleman seems to have modified his proposition this year. Last year he did not come out fiat footed in favour of government ownership ; but this year I believe that both he and some of the hon. gentlemen behind him have come out in favour of government ownership. When the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Putteei moved a resolution last year on the lines of government ownership, many of these gentlemen, who are to-day advocating government ownership did not support him. But I understand that the scales have since fallen from their eyes, including the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), and they now think government ownership would be a good thing. Speakingas. n Wft&teim man, I think it would brTTTore in the interest of the country to have a strong, powerful corporation like the Grand Trunk Railway Company running its lines through the country and giving the people competition for all time to poyne tlnuv-trr~TnTve government ownership if hon. gentlemen opposite got into power. Frorrr'fny~knowledge of how they ran the Intercolonial Railway some years ago, government ownershipwould then mean Canadian Pacific Railway control! That is whaTTfiSTJeopie-crf the Northwest want to escape from. We want competition -actual competition.	.
I am afraid that under the government ownership, which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition would give us, we would not get that competition. Supposing there should be a change of government and hon. gentlemen opposite took office, with a couple of Canadian Pacific Railway directors as cabinet ministers. I would like to know what kind of competition the people of the west would secure from government ownership. We have a government railway as it is, which these hon. gentlemen controlled during the eighteen years they were in office. Mow did they run that railway ? They let it run into decay. They let it end in a buckwheat field-near the city of Quebec. They never made a move to bring it to Montreal where it could compete for freight. They never thought of extending it to Georgian BajT or anywhere else, but actually subsidized another road to run through the state of Maine for the purpose of competing with it. They actually assisted the Canadian Pacific Railway to build a short line through

the state of Maine down to our maritime provinces in order that it might take away trade from the Intercolonial Railway. Anil then they leased to the Canadian Pacific Railway the best paying part of the Intercolonial Railway. With What result 1 With the result that the Canadian Pacific Railway started their trains from the different stations half an hour ahead of the Intercolonial, and took up everything along the route, express, freight and passengers, then the Intercolonial Railway came junketing along in charge of a conductor and a couple of brakesmen, burning up coal and doing no business. That is not the kind of competition we want out in the west. When we see lion, gentlemen opposite, who have been in this House the past twenty years, and who, during all that time, have been opposing, in season and out of season, in the strongest possible manner, government ownership-when we see these men change front in the short space of twelve months and come out in favour of government ownership, we are inclined to view their professions with some suspicion, and we cannot help coming to the conclusion that these hon. gentlemen are inspired in their sudden change by the Canadian Pacific Railway authorities. Should the government scheme go through, the Canadian Pacific Railway will have to encounter live competition, but should hon. gentlemen opposite have their way, and should a government controlled by them own the road, then the Canadian Pacific Railway would be again on top. That is the way I look at the matter from a west* ern standpoint. I would rather a thousand times over have the Grand Trunk Pacific build the road under proper government control, such as this contract provides for, than have the kind of government owned road we might expect if hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. Why should I come to that conclusion ? Why, Mr. Chairman, every move made in the last two years by hon.' gentlemen opposite has been a Canadian Pacific Railway move. Last year they wanted us to buy7 some 636 miles of useless road, with high grades and short curves, running along the north shore of Lake Superior-a road which is a white elephant on the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. They wanted us to buy that road from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and there can be no doubt that we would, in that event, have had to pay the Canadian Pacific Railway $36,000,000 for it. And that is a road which the Canadian Pacific Railway do not need, because they have the Soo line, which gives them the outlet they require. That road, however, hon. gentlemen opposite would like to buy and convert into a government road. But if the Canadian Pacific Railway cannot operate it at a profit, how is the government going to do that ? That was a Canadian Pacific Railway move No. 1. Only the other night I heard these gentlemen getting up one after another and advocating the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific right at once across the prairies. It was rather strange to see these hon, gentlemen take such a sudden interest in the people of the west. But if we look behind the scenes, we will find that the reason they are so anxious to have that done is because the Canadian Pacific Railway owns the spout. You may build all the roads vou like on the prairie, so long as the Canadian Pacific Railway own the spout from the city of Winnipeg to the east, the people of the west will get no relief, because, when you come to the spout, everything has to go through it. The same thing applies to the road further west. That would equally suit the Canadian Pacific Railway, because, if constructed at once, it would be a feeder to that line. That again was another move in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Now we find these hon. gentlemen wanting government ownership. That is another move to benefit the Canadian Pacific Railway. If these hon. gentlemen had control of a government road to the west, the same thing would occur as did occur in the past, and we would have that government road run in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If the leader of the opposition could carry out his proposition to buy this rocky piece of road along the north shore of Lake Superior, some 636 miles, which would cost $36,000,000 of the people's money, what would that mean ? It would mean the handicapping of the government road at once, so that it could not compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The hon. gentleman wanted the government to purchase a road which every one knows is far from being up to date. Take that line to-day, and the best locomotive they can put on it' will only haul eighteen cars of cattle, whereas on the Grand Trunk Railway, between Chicago and Port Huron, one locomotive can haul thirty-five cars of cattle, and the new Grand Trunk Pacific, with the grades specified in this contract, will be able to do the same. That shows that the hon. gentleman's proposition would handicap the government road right at the start. But hon. gentlemen opposite have been very careful not to give too much explanation of their leader's scheme. Last year it fell like a wet blanket on the House. Hon. gentlemen opposite told us we could not have running powers over" other roads. They said that running powers were a myth, and it was no use talking about them. But since then we have had their leader proposing running powers over two lines from Port Arthur to Winnipeg. Last year he came down with a proposition to build a road, but hon. gentlemen opposite did not enthuse over it to any great extent, and have not taken much pains to explain it. There are two propositions before the country. There is the proposition of the right hon. the First Minister, which has been explained over and over again, and then there is the proposition of the

leader of the opposition. But these hon. gentlemen have not taken the pains to explain their proposition. In that they have not followed the example set by the government, and I have no doubt that if the leader of the opposition, instead of wasting time with tu'-penny ha'penny criticisms on the policy of the government, would explain his own-if he would let the country know what he proposes to give the Canadian Pacific Railway for that piece of road on the north shore of Lake Superior and what ho proposes to pay the Canadian Northern for the renting of their road, also what he proposes to pay for the prairie and mountain sections and the Canada Atlantic Railway, he would throw a little more light on the subject; and if he did I am confident that the people would have no difficulty in coming to a decision in favour of the government proposition as against his. The ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) does not appear to approve of either scheme. He wants us to give all our attention to the water-ways. He says that the people of the United States are going to spend $100,000,000 on the Erie canal. That may be, the hon. gentleman is better informed than I am. I know that such a proposition was before the legislative assembly of the state of New York and may have gone through. That canal, however, after it is built, will be only open some six months in the year. Unfortunately, in our northern country our canals freeze over in the winter so that during these six months the hon. gentleman would have the whole trade of the country tied up. I am of the same mind with regard to canals as my hon. friend. I think they will do good work. During navigation we will use them, but we cannot move the crops of the Northwest Territories that we are growing now and what we will grow in the future through the canals. The whole trade of the country cannot be tied up six months in a year. If something be not done, the very object my hon. friend has in view, the building up of a great Canadian nationality, will fall to the ground, because you will divert the trade across the boundary to the United States if you do not open and build this^ road, and do it quickly.
Now, what does it mean? It means that if you build the government road through that northern country as a colonization road, and also to give connection with the west, you must look for business for that road to do. Well, where are your feeders; where are your connections? The provinces of Ontario and Quebec are grid-ironed with railways to-day, and those railways are in the hands of two companies, practically. Suppose you have a government road built through to the Northwest. Freight will be gathered up by the Grand Trunk in every city, town, village and hamlet that it touches, and carried to the Northwest through American channels. And the' Canadian Pacific Railway will collect freight from all the many places Mr.' DAVIS.
with which they connect and will run it over their own system. Where, then, is this government road that hon. gentlemen eposite talk about going to find anything to do? We have heard about deficits on government roads before, but they are nothing to what we would have on nuch a road as this. The effect of this contract will be to place the people of eastern Canada, every community whether small or great, in touch with the people of the west; and it will have this effect at once. Every little hamlet in Ontario will be able to send its goods and manufactures through to the Northwest.
Will the hon. member (Mr. Davis) allow me to ask him a question?
Certainly.
Does not freight for the Northwest, originating in towns in the east, go right tlirougn to its destination?

Over the Canadian Pacific Pacific Railway and it takes in many cases seven months to get there. I have pointed out that in the town in which I live we have not had any freight since last January. If lion, gentlemen imagine that the people of tile Northwest will put up with that state of affairs they are quite wrong.
You cannot stop floods.
This is not a case of floods. There were no floods in January, nor were there any' in February or March.
There was snow.

There was snow, certainly. But the railway companies of this country know that there is going to be snow in the winter, and they should be prepared for it when it comes. There is such a thing as building snow fences; there is such a thing as having enough coal for their locomotives; there is such a thing as recognizing that the winter brings snow and getting ready for it. One winter's experience should be enough, instead of having this kind of thing occur year after year. But I was showing the absurdity of the proposition of the leader of the hon. gentlemen opposite. I was showing that even if he built this government road that he speaks of, it would have nothing to do. I suppose that even freight carried by the Canadian Pacific Railway from the east would go through by the United States, because if mis middle portion of the line around Lake Superior, were taken over by the government, the Canadian Pacific Railway would run their freight through the American side line on the Soo. And so, all the freight collected in this country would be taken out through American territory. I suppose that portions of this government road would be a colonization road. But, as for through-freight, it

lias never been explained so that I can understand it, where the freight is coining from that it is to carry from the eastern country to the west. And. if this government road were run by hon. gentlemen *opposite as they ran the existing government road when they were in power, the whole thing would turn out a pretty tough proposition, I am afraid. And, so far as the Northwest is concerned, we would still have the Canadian Pacific Railway on our backs, like the old man of the sea. We are trying to throw him off. We want competition-good live competition: and the way to get it is by the construction of this road. So far as this contract is concerned, it seems to me it is pretty fair. Let hon. gentlemen opposite compare it with the contract that their party made for the construction of a great railway some years ago I do not forget that that was at a time when conditions were not as favourable as they are now. But even allowing a large margin for that, this is a far better contract. So far as the western part of this road ig concerned, it is true that this government guarantees three-quarters of the cost. But then the government have a mortgage, and. K tlle contract is not carried out, the road will belong to the people. The eastern portion of the road is to be built by the government and handed over to the Grand Trunk to operate for fifty years. , The hon member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) said that in the House a day or so ago. that after a company began operation of a road they would have to spend $10,000 a mile on it in a few years to get it in good shape. If that is the case, then, the Grand Trunk will have to spend a great deal of money m the future in improving the road ; so I fancy that when the road is handed back to the government it will be worth three times as much as when the Grand Trunk took hold of it. So. we will have three per cent interest on the money spent in constructing, we will open and develop a new territory, we will give a new outlet to the people of the west and, when we get the road back it wili be a property greatly increased in value. Then, so far as this railway is concerned, there is no exemption fropi taxation. These people are going to bear their share of the burdens of the country like the rest of us. There is full control of rates retained by the government, so that oppression of the People in that way is impossible.
Now, I would like to say a word about a statement of the leader of the oposition as to the stock of this road. He says that even if the stock is sold at ten cents on the dollar, the freight rates would be made high enough to pay the interest on the par value. But, if he looks at the records of the United States, he will find that not half the railways of that country pay dividends on the stock. There is a railway commission for every state, and you have
the interstate commission besides, and these authorities do not take the stock into consideration in fixing the rates. They count the bonds as being the money that built the road, while the stock represents the speculative element, and the stock is not taken into consideration in settling the rates of transportation. Nor will it be in this case, I think. So long as the road is not bonded at too high a figure the stock does not matter so much. The eastern part of this road is to be built by the government, and it is to their interest to build as cheaply as possible. And, as the Grand Trunk have to pay interest on the cost after ten years, they also will try to keep down the expense of construction. I venture to say, though I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, that the company will be able to pay that interest and make a good return for themselves during the time this contract runs. This country is advancing rapidly. We are bringing in at least 128,000 people a year to fill up our unoccupied territory, and that number is not going to diminish. The production of wealth is increasing by leaps and bounds. Surely, with the progress Canada is making we can afford to have another outlet to the east. Surely we are not always going to be hung like a fringe along the edge of the rivers and lakes, but are to have depth as well as breadth to our country. This road will give us depth. I do not pretend to know about the northern country, but I do know about the western. That country has passed the experimental stage. We know what-it is producing and will produce. We are in a position now to say that the western provinces of this country will occupy the same relation to the eastern provinces that the western and middle states occupy to the eastern states at this time. Practically the whole wealth of the United States is concentrated in the western and middle states, and the same state of things will be brought about in this country. Let hon. gentlemen opposite explain to us the policy that they advocate in contrast with this, and not confine themselves to the small criticism we hear in connection with this Bill. We challenge them to explain their scheme. Let them put it in their newspapers and explain to the people what they propose to do. But no, they keep harping away about such little things as the building of this prairie section inside of three years. Any reasonable person understands that that prairie section must be built before the mountain section can be touched. They have only eight years in which to build the whole road, and it must necessarily fellow that they will build the prairie section in three years, because that leaves them only five years for the Rocky Mountain section. They know that, but in order to lead the public to believe that there was something wrong they keep on with

this petty criticism day by day. I would like them to explain their position and if they take the proposition of the leader ef the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and place it alongside that of the government, I have ro fear of the result. I think the people of this country will decide quickly that this contract will be much more in the interest of Canada than the one which the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has proposed.
I am dealing with the project which is submitted to us by the government.
What about the other one

None of your business.
cr untry is bordering on the American states, where'there is already a complete system cr railways. How many times have I heard try hou. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Davis) suggest that the trade of tae Northwest might go to American ports.
I say that now.

I say that also. That is the main Point. The Grand Trunk is located on the other side of the line. My right hon. friend and his colleagues tell us they will prevent the American railways from taking the trade from us by building a road 1.900 miles long. That cannot be done. Build your road, as you have made up your minds to do so, but supplement your policy by something else.

When the hon. member lor Halifax (Mr. It. L. Borden) is in office, if I am a member of this House and if he ermes down with a proposition I will deal ^ ith it then. 1 have heard a good many business men discussing this question in the last few weeks. They are trying to understand the ministerial project. As to the proposition made last year and the other one made this year by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). I for one do not feel justified in dealing with it row.
Keep away from it.

It is enough for me, in my humbleness, to deal with a strong govern ment; I feel it enough now. It is no vse trying to draw herrings across the track. We are discussing a very grave matter indeed, and the question to which I have tried to call attention has not yet been grappled nvith. The Grand Trunk is two-fold ; it has its system between Chi cago. Buffalo and Portland. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his colleagues have not explained in what way they will be able to force the Grand Trunk to send Canadian traffic through Canadian channels. It has not been explained as yet, I should like to have it explained. The plan of the leader of the opposition is one thing which may be submitted later on, but as far as I could see, the government will carry the day now, their project will certainly be adopted. There is no doubt about that. How is the government going to arrange matters so that Canadian trade, especially that of the Canadian Northwest, will not be diverted to the existing Grand Trunk lines on the American side? This is the main point of the discussion, in my view. The Prime Minister has said, and so have some of his colleagues, that they want to send the trade of the west to the maritime provinces and to Quebec. I say that the present scheme cannot succeed unless it is supplemented in some way. We cannot lose sight of the fact that our Northwest

The hon. gentleman is talking about a road 1.900 miles long from M in-nipeg ho the Atlantic ocean. Let him estimate the distance from Winnipeg to the ocean by the route which he fears u ill get the trade, and see how the comparison stands. All wheat has to go to the Atlantic.

The point I am making is clear to any one who wants to discuss this matter from a business standpoint. The Grand Trunk Railway has a line built from Chicago to Buffalo and Portland, a complete and fully organized system of railway from Chicago. By building a short line or by making running arrangements between Duluth and Chicago, with some existing line, they will be able to obtain a road 900 miles to Chicago, where they will join their existing lines, and will have not to spend a cent further. Is it not clear that their interest is to divert as much trade as they can to their existing lines, in order to pay better dividends to their shareholders? We cannot blame them; trade has no love. They are there on the American soil, they have their American ports. My friend is speaking of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He sees the Canadian Pacific Railway everywhere, but lie must not forget one thing, that the Canadian Pacific Railway is essentially a Canadian railway, built on Canadian soil, they have not settled in Portland, they have settled in St. John, N.B. He has reproached the late government with having given them a subsidy to go to the maritime provinces. He should not forget, nobody should forget, that that short line between Montreal and St. John has been subsidized so as to enable the Canauian Pacific Railway to compete with American lines in taking trade to Canadian ports. I am glad my hon. friend from the Northwest has brought up the Canadian Pacific Railway once more. The Canadian Pacific Railway has vast connections in the Northwest. It comes down to the head of Lake Superior, it goes down through

the most fertile parts and through the great centres of trade of Ontario and Quebec. It goes to Toronto, to Montreal, crosses the St. Lawrence and on to port of St. John.
I know as a positive fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway are spending half a million dollars a year by going to the port of St. John, that they would have by not going. Still, they are passing through two large provinces and they are tapping large centres of trade. Where is the trade of the northern line which is going to be built to come from ? My hon. friend says that we must not be isolated for six months in the year. I grant all that. I do not object to the Grand Trunk Railway Company going to the Northwest, but I ask the government to find the means that will make the Canadian trade of the Northwest go through Canadian channels. That is all I want. The position is a very dangerous one. It is not the fault of the Grand Trunk Railway managers. The location of the Grand Trunk Railway is settled for all time. I cannot say too often or too loudly that it is part an American railway and part a Canadian railway. Their winter port is at Portland. It will always be their winter port. It cannot be anything else. We made it ourselves. The question is whether the government have been wise in insisting that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall control altogether this new enterprise. Public ownership has been alluded to on many occasions. As it is six o'clock I shall say a word or two on this subject after recess.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
