This afternoon I reminded the House of the fact, that the Grand Trunk is partly an American and partly a Canadian railway. That is not their fault, but is nevertheless a fact, and we cannot lose sight of it in this discussion. I have prepared a short memorandum of the distances I referred to this afternoon. From Winnipeg to Duluth the distance on a straight line is 360 miles ; from Duluth to Ashland ou the Wisconsin Central 76 miles ; from Ashland to Chicago 437 miles, or a total of 873 miles from Winnipeg to Chicago. It is estimated that a road could be built from Winnipeg to Duluth and thence to Ashland for $35,000 per mile, but for the purposes of my calculation I shall place it at $40,000. The road from Winnipeg to Duluth would therefore cost $14,400,000 ; and from Duluth to Ashland $3,400,000 ; total $17,800,000. The Grand Trunk Railway Company-if they have not done so already-could get possession of the Wisconsin Central from Ashland to Chicago for $13,000,000, which would make all told a sum of $30,000,000. which it would be necessary for the Grand Trunk to invest to get a
straight line from Winnipeg to Chicago. Let us say that they will pay four per cent for that money which will not be guaranteed by the Canadian government. That will give them an annual interest charge to meet of $1,200,000. When they reach Chicago they are in their own territory, connecting with their own line which is fully equipped, and the trade from the Canadian Northwest would simply add value to that line as a first class feeder. What is the position of the Grand Trunk in relation to the government project 1 From Winnipeg to Moncton the distance is in round numbers 1.900. Time v\ ill tell whether I am right or wrong, but my own conviction is that that line will cost $50,000 a mile to construct; however I will put it at $40,000 a mile. That would make $76,000,000 on which, at three per cent, the Grand Trunk Pacific would have to pay an annual interest amounting to $2,280,000. In view of this, I ask every businessman of the country to tell where the interest of the Grand Trunk Company lies. Are they going to lose $1,000,000 a year for the love of Canada ?	Is it not in
the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to take the trade of the Northwest to their own line ? What business man will gainsay that proposition. I approve of the GrarnTPruuk entering into the Northwest. Thev are anxious to go there, and the Minister of Justice stated a great truth when he reminded the House, that the prairie section of the Grand Trunk Pacific will he a very paying line. The Canadian Pacific Railway are tohlay building branches without a sking^any Assistance from this parliament.
What branches ?
I cannot name them, but my hon. friend knows that they are building branches right and left.
I do not know.
Are they building any branches ?
They are and getting subsidies for them-name your branches.

I have not the names on my fingers' ends to-night, but the Canadian Pacific Railway are building some branches without asking for subsidies. Of course they would be glad to have subsidies given ; any railroad would. However that argument is not essential to my case, and I will dismiss it. I agree with the Minister of Justice, that the government will perhaps never have to pay a dollar for the guarantee on the prairie section, because it will pay as na business enterprise. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will build that part of the line as quickly as they can ; they will centre in Winnipeg as then1 western terminal. From Winnipeg are they going to take the trade to their American lines which I have just described ; or will they take it over the

government line, or will they take a good deal of it through the lakes in the summer months ? All sensible men who have studied the question, agree that in summer time it is out of question that these long stretches of railway can compete with water carriage. I am glad to see the right hon. the Prime Minister now in his seat, and for his benefit I will repeat the figures which I have already given. I say this seriously, because a public man such as he is has not the time to study these questions from all points of view.
The Grand Trunk is at Chicago, and it requires a little over S00 miles to connect the Chicago, Buffalo and Portland line with Winnipeg. I say again, I do not see how the Grand Trunk Railway Company can do otherwise than favour their American connections in the winter mouths. Portland is their port. The distance from Winnipeg to Portland is in round numbers 2,000 miles, against 1,900 miles from Winnipeg to Moncton which is not of course a sea-port. The Grand Trunk will run on its own lines* which are already built, for a distance of 1,138 miles, without spending one cent of additional money. It seems to me that these figures, which cannot be successfully contradicted, are very important in the present discussion. Well, what are we going to do ? The government have made up their minds to build the eastern division. They say it will be a great colonization road.
I hope it will be. I hope I shall live long enough to see it a successful colonization road. But it cannot be a successful commercial road now or for many years. I have reminded the House of the position of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is tapping all the important centres of trade in Canada. It as also an important feeder in the Soo line. I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) refer to the Canadian Pacific Railway branches on American soil in a disparaging way. They are feeders to the main line on Canadian soil ; they are nothing else. And let me say within the hearing of the business men of the country that without the Soo line I doubt very much whether the Canadian Pacific Railway would be in a position to go to the Canadian port of St. John. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan says : We cannot be isolated. That is not the point. Nobody desires to see the Northwest isolated. It is not isolated to-day. It is better served with railways than any other part of the country. In my own province we are not served as well. We know that we have a great realm there, and we want to develop it; but we want to develop it in the interest of Canada, and it is only fair that we should do so. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan and the members of the government, with the right hon. gentleman at their head, have alluded to the Asiatic trade. We have heard able arguments

on that subject. Will my right hon. friend kindly pay attention to the present state of affairs in China and Japan, so far as trade is concerned ? The trade of China last year amounted to $330,000,000, imports and exports, and the trade of Japan amounted to $250,000,000. In listening to the arguments on this subject, one would suppose that those countries had no fertile lands. Manchuria, Mongolia and Siberia have just as much wheat lands as we have. They are only beginning to develop their lands and trade. They have done marvellous things thus far. Last year Siberia exported to the English market $15,000,000 worth of butter. It can grow wheat, corn and everything that we can, it can raise cattle. In a few years, when we have peace-and let us hope we shall have it soon-all these countries will be producing and exporting. I am afraid we shall not be able to export to them much wheat or butter or cheese. We may expect to export manufactured articles. But we are not alone in that. The Americans, the English, the Germans and the French have already taken a firm hold there. Then, Canadian trade is not yet much in sight. The Grand Trunk Pacific will certainly take from Asia, tea, rice and articles of that kind and we may send to Asia manufactured articles to a certain extent. But it will take many years to develop that trade. I will not discuss at any length that part of the scheme. It may materalize all right. The government guarantee the interest on 75 per cent of the cost of the road. The Grand Trunk authorities believe that it will be eighteen years before they will have to pay any interest on 75 per cent of the cost. Well, I will dismiss that part of the enterprise. I desire to confine my remarks to the position of Canada, so far as the trade of the Grand Trunk is concerned. I verily believe that unless the government supplement their policy to-day with a strong and energetic water-way policy, their present policy will be a destructive one. I would hope time will prove that I am wrong ; but that is my candid opinion, for this excellent reason, that railways cannot compete with water-ways, and the summer season is the season of trade, both export and import. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan asked us this afternoon whether there would not be a large import trade. Let us look at the records of this country. The import trade of St. John represents only 20 per cent of the export trade in the winter months. Our hon. friends who are in the grain trade know very well that the export of grain is mostly carried out by railway's and water-ways in the summer time. Some of our hon. friends say that a good deal of American grain is carried from Chicago to New York. Let them look at the records of the export of grain. There is very little grain exported in the winter months. American railways carry grain in the winter months for local con-

sumption, to a very large extent at any rate. Then, what I humbly suggest to the government is that they do not go too fast. They have pledged the administration to building the Transcontinental Railway. My right hon. friend is entitled to be a proud man. He has been a very successful political man ; and I quite understand that he may desire to have his name associated with a great transcontinental railway. I don not blame him for such an ambition. But is it not the part of prudence to go slowly, at any rate so far as a certain part of the enterprise is concerned V The Grand Trunk Railway would not undertake themselves to build the road from Winnipeg down to the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I was in the Railway Committee when that question came up, and the Grand Trunk Railway would not, undertake to do this, because they thought it would not be a paying enterprise. From their standpoint they were right. They were not eager either, to build that part of the road from the Rockies. They were anxious to get a charter, but were not anxious to go on immetli-ately with that enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

They wished to get a share in the development of the Northwest and to be in a position to handle their own traffic east and west. We are all agreed that they should be put in that position. But I wish to ask my right hon. friend to pause before undertaking to build that part of the railway between Winnipeg and the maritime provinces. I know that what I am saying will be interpreted by opponents as being inimical to the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces. I am used to that kind of argument, and am not afraid to say what I think is right. There will be a survey before that enterprise is undertaken. That survey will last a couple of years, at any rate more than a year. When we have that survey, if it be demonstrated that there are large tracks of good, arable land in that section, I will stand by the scheme myself, from the point of view of colonization. I do not believe in it as a commercial enterprise, but will stand by it as a colonization road, although I am quite prepared to admit that there are many other and better ways of developing colonization. But it will serve, to a limited extent, as a comercial enterprise, and to a great extent as a colonization enterprise, should there be in that country large quantities of arable land. These are my views on the question before the House.
Some of my hon. friends ask me what I think of public ownership. In the position I occupy. I have no hesitation in saying what I think. I am free to speak my mind. The question of public owner-ship is not a new one. Not only has it been discussed, but it has been tested. Out of 220,000 mites
of railway, which are in operation in the world outside of the United States, there are about 160,000 miles which are owned by governments and administered by states. The railways in Germany, Russia, Belgium, Holland, Australia are all owned by the respective governments of these countries. In other words, the countries in which there are government owned railways are countries where the government owns them all. In France the government has practically built the railways. It has guaranteed the money required to build them, and the railways become gradually the pi-operty of the state. Its Minister of Public Works has full and complete control of the rates ; and these rates, moreover, are regulated by the fact that the government own and possess 12,000 miles of canals, which are indeed a great regulator of rates, so far as railways are concerned. In Germany many people may suppose that the roads are administered from a military standpoint, that is not the case. When Bismarck undertook to buy the railways of the German states, he had no doubt in view the military interests of the empire, but he had specially in view its commercial interests. In 1901 the net profits on the 32,000 miles of German railways were $178,000,000. In Germany the state owns all the railways, and Germany has a population of over 50,000,000 people. In Russia-I do not speak of the Siberian Railway-there are 30,000 miles of railway, also owned by the state.' The government of Russia owns all the railways, and they are a paying property. In Germany the state earns about six per cent interest on the money invested. In Russia about the same. In Belgium the government last year earned about three and a half or four per cent on the amount Invested. And the rates in those countries are a great deal lower than they are in England, where the railways are not owned by the state. It must be remembered .that in those countries all the railways are owned by the state. It would be difficult to own one railway, as is proposed, in this country. We have subsidized the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Northern, and many other companies. Suppose we own a railway, we would either make it a paying business, and in that case we would be obliged to charge rates that would yield a good return, or we would have to face a heavy annual deficit. Then it would be very difficult indeed not to charge the same rates ns other companies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Because, if we were to charge lower rates, we would simply ruin all the other companies. The question is not a new one for my former colleagues and myself, and I may be now defending opinions which I advocated in the past. This is an interesting question indeed, but we are not called on to discuss it now. It is true, the leader

250S
of the opposition has placed a suggestion before the House.
Let its hear about that.

I say, that this is but a political argument and not a business argument. My bon. friend will admit that. We are now discussing a business matter. We are discussing the government project, With part of if I agree, I shall not lose much time in discussing the details. The Grand Trunk Railway have no doubt obtained an advantageous agreement. But what I am anxious about is the fact that my right hon. friend and his colleagues place so much importance on leaving the entire control of the enterprise in the hands of a company which is partly American and partly Canadian. That is the danger, and it is a great danger. Let my words be weighed by those who have studied the question and who have no party interest to serve. My right hon. friend and his colleagues may avert the danger to a certain extent by properly equipping now our-water-ways. They may in this way avert the danger to a pretty large extent; but let them not forget that unless they do so, they will have to fight against American railways and American water-ways.

The hon. gentleman gives us to understand that by constructing or purchasing a road from Winnipeg to Chicago, the Grand Trunk Railway would have a through road from Winnipeg via Chicago to Portland, which would only be a hundred miles longer than by the Canadian road to Moncton.
Yes.
And that by sending their freight over their road by Chicago they would save over a million dollars a year ?
Yes.

That being the case, why is it that the Grand Trunk people, who are certainly good business men, have anything to do with the construction of this Grand Trunk Pacific road, when they are going to save $1,000,000 a year by going by the other route ?

I am very glad indeed that my hon. friend has called my attention to that point

which.' however, was on my memorandum. What is the amount the Grand Trunk Railway Company are putting into this enterprise? The Grand Trunk Railway Company have made a good bargain. I congratulate them. They have acquired the control of the whole transcontinental railway without putting money into it. That is the position.
And they have done it in order that they may injure their own road?

My hon. friend is a sound
business man
No.

Yes, he is a sound business man. He has sound judgment; I know him well. It is greatly to the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to gain access to the Northwest

Mr. WRIGHT, But they could go by the other route-

Will my hon. friend permit me? The Grand Trunk Railway Company, as I have said is a two-fold company. They have an outlet in Chicago and an outlet in Montreal and an outlet in Buffalo and an outlet in Portland. Between Chicago and Portland they own a magnificent piece of railway 1,138 miles long. They own also a system of railways in Canada. They have a strong incentive, then, to gain access to the Northwest. They asked for a charter; they wanted to build a road from a certain point in the province of Ontario to the Rocky mountains. My hon. friend (Mr. Wright) is a member of the Railway Committee and he remembers the debate. The Grand Trunk Railway Company secured the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company without putting any money into it, .the government agreeing to build from Winnipeg to Moncton at their own expense, borrowing the money for that purpose and renting the line, when completed, not to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, mind you, but to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, a company that the Grand Trunk controls, but into which it has put no money.
They have to pay three per cent on the cost of the road.

The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have to pay three per cent, but the Grand Trunk Railway Company have not to pay anything, have they? They pay no money toward the enterprise, and yet they control it. They have invested a very large amotfht of money in their system from Chicago to Portland, have they not? And on that they have to pay not only working expenses, but dividends as well. But on the railway between Winnipeg and Moncton they will not have a dollar to pay. The bargain is that three per cent shall be paid. Very well. If the Grand Trunk Pacific is a paying business they will pay three per cent ; but if it is not' a paying business, they will not pay. And we can not complain. I expect-and I do not blame the government for it ; I am very frank in saying that-I expect not only that we shall receive no interest for the ten years provided for in the contract, but, perhaps for another ten years and perhaps more. I do not say that we shall have to bear the whole interest, but I would be very much and very agreeably surprised if. before I die, I find that piece of railway

paying three per cent. I appeal to the business men of the country on that point.
However, I am not discussing the financial aspect of the question. I am addressing myself to the national aspect-the question of the future of the country. If I am wrong, in my financial calculations, if the road between Winnipeg and Moncton pays three per cent after ten years, I shall be glad. I do not expect it, but I shall be glad if my expectation is not realized. But that is not the great point at issue. 1 invite my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his colleagues to deal with this matter in a businesslike way. The great point; at issue, is where is the trade of Canada to go when that line of railway is completed?
To Quebec.
Will it go to Quebec in the summer months?
Yes.

Well, when we know that grain is being carried by water from Duluth 1Quebec for less than three cents per bushel, and a business man like my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) says that the prospective railway will carry the grain from the Northwest to Quebec, I have no answer to give. The answer is in the minds of all business men. My hon. friend (Mr. Heyd), is not serious, i know. In the summer months Quebec will get trade by the water-ways. I hope that navigation at Quebec in future will be kept open a little longer than it has been in the past. I expect that that will be the case. In the winter months the trade will not go to Quebec. Our friends from the maritime provinces expect it, and if there is any trade they must get it, because Quebec is closed during the winter. No. The old city of Quebec has a great prospect, but it is bound up with the carrying out of the policy of water-ways. We must not neglect railways, of course, but I say that, from a commercial standpoint the St. Lawrence route, that is to say, the water-ways, are the route par excellence. I do not know what the government will do; I am not in their secrets. But it seems to me they have ahead of them a clear-cut policy. Let them build this road, if, after the surveys are made they decide to do so. But. even before they have made up their minds fully to build the eastern section of this road, let them make up their minds to develop our water-ways to the fullest extent. Let them equip our harbours; let them help the organization of the railways from the Georgian Bay down; let them apply their energy and ability to completing and improving the St. Lawrence route from one end to the other. I believe that my suggestion is a good one, that it is a practical one: and I am inclined to believe that the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will not dismiss it without giving it a careful second thought.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Though the-observations of my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) are not at all germane to the paragraph in the contract we have before us, still, as we have not, for some time, had the pleasure of listening to my hon. friend,. I am sure we are all willing to stretch the rules a little for the pleasure of listening to his observations. But I must say to my hon. friend that I have listened to him [DOT]with some surprise. He is not the same man I used to know. He used to be strongly national in his aspirations. Now, he advises me to look at the map of the continent. If that advice and what went with it meant anything at all, it meant that, looking at the map of the continent, the government w-ould not build this railway but would allow trade to take its natural course.
If we were to look at the map and to take into account only geographical considerations this railway would not be built-no Canadian railways would have been built. If in the past we had looked at the map and regarded geographical considerations alone the railways of Canada, instead of running east and west, would have run north and south. This the natural consequence of the advice of my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) has given me that we should observe the position in which we are placed, that the American harbours are nearer to the wheat fields of the west than the Canadian harbours, and that therefore we should allow the trade to go to the nearest harbours and not force it to the more distant ones. My hon. friend Air. Tarte) in the course of his remarks this afternoon recalled the discussion which took place in 1849, when the Grand Trunk project was first brought to the attention of the country. He recalled the mistake made by Sir George Cartier-who, I am proud to sav was a Canadian of the Canadians-he recalled the fact that Sir George Cartier made the great mistake of considering the geography of the country, looking only at the map and not at national consideration and favoured Portland in foreign territory instead of some port in British territory as the terminus of the road. If Sir George Cartier had then followed the policy we are now following, of not observing the map except in order to rectify the features of geography that are against us, Portland would not have been made the winter terminus of the Grand Trunk Railway, but probably some maritime province port would have been selected. The policy we have in view is to endeavour to correct the mistakes of the past, to force the Grand Trunk Company to have a harbour in Canadian waters, as well as a harbour in American waters. We cannot undo the past altogether ; Portland has been made the winter terminus of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I do not expect that they are going to abandon what they have. I expect, on the contrary, that Portland will serve the Grand Trunk as a winter port for the trade that they now have.

But I expect that the trade of the future which is to be gathered by the Grand Trunk in the west will be brought down to some Canadian harbour on the Atlantic shore. At all events that is our policy.
Sir, my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) stated a moment ago that we should not forget the St. Lawrence route and the water-ways, that the water route after all, is the most natural. There is no doubt about one thing that in summer time, all railways in the west wTill seek the water just as the duck seeks the wrnter. Trade will go by water route in summer. I wish to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) although the water-way is the more natural, does it follow that where you have a water-way you are not to have any railway communication ? I may say that our policy is not at all antagonistic to the policy he is laying down, the development of the waterways. The two should go hand in hand together. I would be sorry to say that the policy wTe are advocating at the present time, of another transcontinental railway, should be held up by myself as against the development of our water-ways. On the contrary, we are most clear that we must develop our water-ways and it seems to me that we are doing it at the present time. There is not much more to be done in improving the St. Lawrence. We can improve the channels here and there and facilitate the handling of trade at the terminals, but I do not see that *we can do much more than that. At all events X would like to hear now, or at some other time, what further development my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) advises. If we had followed the policy which my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) now indicates, would we have built the Canadian Pacific Railway ? I doubt it. Why, Sir, we should have allowed the trade to go to the American harbours. It would have been as short for the Canadian Pacific Railway to take the trade by the southern as by the northern shore of Lake Superior. When the Canadian Pacific Railway charter was passed in 1880 and 1881, the parliament of Canada gave the Canadian Pacific Railway the power to go both north and south of Lake Superior. The first railway which penetrated the Northwest came from American territory and at the present time there is trade, I am glad to say, for the Canadian Pacific Railway on both shores of Lake Superior. Of course the Grand Trunk will develop it's trade by the north shore, but why is it that the Grand Trunk when they first put their proposition before parliament, forgetting all the advantages which my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) has just brought to my attention, asked to be allowed to penetrate the Northwest Territories, not by the south shore of Lake Superior, but by the north shbre-because my hon. friend remembers and knows very well that the first proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway was to build from North Bay to Winnipeg, on the north shore of Lake Superior. According to the statements of my Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
hon. friend a moment ago, it would have been easier and cheaper for the Grand Trunk to penetrate into the Northwest Territories by the south than by the north shore of Lake Superior.
Lake Superior ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, if I correctly understood my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) he stated the company could by easy stages open a line from Winnipeg to Duluth and from Duluth to Chicago. The Grand Trunk may or may not have that power, but they value the advantage of penetrating into the Northwest on Canadian soil, they wanted to bring that trade to Portland. But there the difference between them and us came in. We told them that we would not agree, and that unless they agreed and consented to bring their line over Canadian territory to the harbours on the Canadian shore of the ocean, we would not enter into any arrangement with them. What is the inducement to the Grand Trunk Railway Company to do this ? The reason that they agree to pay 3 per cent upon the cost of the line from Winnipeg is that they expect to develop trade upon, that part of the road. They expect there will be valuable local traffic upon that road. As to the character of the country along the proposed road so far as agriculture is concerned, we have no information of any consequence at this moment ; I admit that. But we have information which cannot be gainsaid that there are upon that section of the northern part of this country valuable forests, that there are water powers of unknown quantity, and that there are indications of very valuable mineral deposits. If we have in that northern country water powers, forests, and minerals we have everything required to give local traffic for that road. At all events the Grand Trunk have so much confidence in the enterprise that they are ready to lease the line and pay 3 per cent interest upon it. My hon. friend says that he will not discuss the financial aspect of the matter now, nor shall I. The Grand Trunk control this company. But my hon. friend says they put no money in it. They will have to put some money in it, otherwise they cannot fulfil the contract. At the present time if the enterprise is successful they have to pay 3 per cent for the lease. Why are the Grand Trunk willing to pay 3 per cent on the lease? Because they cannot default upon the payment of the lease of the portion of their line from Winnipeg to Moncton without defaulting on the whole road, and if the whole road is successful they must pay the rent in order to have the valuable western section. At all events that is our expectation and that is the bargain we have made with them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is under obligation to pay 3 per cent on the cost of the road from

Winnipeg to Moncton. I do not find one word in any of the contracts which obliges the Grand Trunk to pay a dollar. Does my right hon. friend know of any section that does ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know that the Grand Trunk is bound under this contract to maintain that line, to control it.
The Grand Trunk ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the Grand Trunk is bound under this agreement (o emtrol the Grand Trunk Pacific, of course, if is to its interest to see that the enterprise is successful. I say that if it wants to take advantage of the line it can take advantage of it, but it must take the good and the bad at the same time. Otherwise if cannot maintain the enterjirise at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: All I wanted ro understand was whether my right hon. friend and 1 were at one as to whether there is any legal obligations whatever on the part of the Grand Trunk to pay any part of the rental.	[DOT]
In case the Grand Tiunk declines to pay the rental of the eastern division, where is the penalty in the contract ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The whole o.' the stock is security for that part of the enterprise. My hon. friend will find tlirt in the contract.
Where is it ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am sorry I have not the clause at hand, but I will show it to my hon. friend in a few minutes. This in a few words, is what I have to say to my hon. friend in regard to this enterprise. Take the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I want to bring this fact to the attention of my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) who wanted to discuss it from a business 1 oint of view. When the Canadian Pacific Railway had reached Montreal, it desired ro have a winter terminus. It would have been quite easy to have followed the line of geography and found an eastern terminus in American territory. The Canadian Pacific Railway might have gone to Portland, or Boston, or to three or four other different ports in the Atlantic shore in American territory. But, it went to a port in Canadian territory. It adopted a line which up to the present time has not given it much profit. Why did it do that 7 It was compelled to do so on account of national sentiment. It was compelled to develop the trade of St. John and although the trade of St. John is not giving much profit to the Canadian Pacific Railway at The present time. I think it is a trade which is very important, and the Canadian Pacific Railway expect in the course of time to make it a very profitable trade. Well. ir is the same consideration which is moving 80
the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Canada, is coming to the front, it is becoming a large country, it is becoming a great country and the Grand Trunk Pacific will find it to its advantage to be a national line as well as the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific will find it to its advantage to have a line upon Canadian territory as well as upon American territory. Of course my hon. friend may say that the Grand Trunk Railway can go to Chicago. So it can, but if it goes to Chicago, it forfeits its rights under the contract, and it takes all the consequences.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before any other member of the committee speaks, I would draw attention to the fact that this discussion which has been going on since eight o'clock is irregular. But, I was just going to say that if the committee is of opinon that it should still go on, I have no particular objection. Still, I want to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that it is not regular.

I have only one word in answer to my right hon. friend's statements. I am very glad indeed that he has told us that the government is not losing sight to-day and will not lose sight in the future, of the great importance of the waterway policy, if I may call it such. We will see before the end of the session what the statement of my right hon. friend means. My right hon. friend will not forget, I am sure, that the Canadian Pacific Railway was under the control of one company. There was no Canadian Pacific Railway Company having a railway partly in Canada and partly in the United. States. It was a Canadian road from beginning to end. It was located on Canadian soil from west to east. I remember just as if it were yesterday the debate which took place in regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and when my right hon. friend was on his feet one of his speeches came 11 my mind. I sent for the book. My right hon. friend then had so little confidence in the connecting line between the west and the east, that in a speech of great eloquence lie suggested that the sectiou upon the north shore of Lake Superior should not be built.
I have the book in my hand. I am very much afraid that we are divided on the same lines to-day as we were then. The Conservative party to which I belonged then - 1 was a newspaper man in those days- wanted to build the railway on Canadian st il from one end of the country to the other. My right hon friend and his friends were suggesting that the section north of Lake Superior might be postponed, and that the Bade would go where it was pleased to go. Put, the idea of a Canadian transcontinental railway tool; hold of the Canadian public (/pinion and the road was built. I say again to my right hon. friend, that I do not ob-



.ieet to the Grand Trunk going into the Northwest, but I ask him, and he has not answered the question, and none of his colleagues have answered it, how he can teil us that the Grand Trunk Railway Company v. hich has its line from Chicago to Buffalo and Portland and which is using that line to a very large extent in handling Canadian tiaffic, is going to be induced to send traffic by this northern line. My right hon. friend and his colleagues cannot point to a single clause of the contract which binds the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to pay three per cent interest. The government will borrow the money. Let us not forget the position. The government lias undertaken to build the line. Well, and good. To build the line it will borrow ihe money on our own credit. We must borrow the money to build the line. We will appoint commissioners, they will build the line, they will pay for the cost of the line and then we will be bound to- pay the interest ourselves. We have made an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, not with the Grand Trunk Rail-v*ay Company, that it will pay three per cent interest after a certain time, but if it does not pay, who is bound to pay ?-The Canadian people are bound to pay. But again I say the financial question is not the one about which I am most anxious. What I am most anxious about is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has every inducement to divert the trade to its American lines, and the government cannot remedy that danger which. is a great one, unless it improves our water-ways immediately. I am very glad that my right bon. friend has taken my remarks in the spirit that dictated them. If he would weigh again the arguments that have been placed before him, not only by myself, but by many business men in connection with our water-ways, I think he would not hesitate even during this session to bring down a policy that would satisfy the country. I believe that the danger is more serious, perhaps, than my right hon. friend has thought. I would remind him again, end this is my last word, of the energetic efforts that the Americans are making in the improvement of their water-ways.- It -costs inside of three cents a bushel for wheat and less for corn on the Erie canal. On the New York Central in the summer time i< costs about four cents a bushel. With the completion of the improvements to the Erie canal and the deepening of St. Mary's river, the Americans will carry grain from Duluth or Chicago to New York, for about two cents a bushel. It costs only one cent and a fraction to take a bushel of wheat from Chicago or Duluth to Buffalo. Mr. Noble, an eminent engineer, believes that with the improved Erie canal, wheat can be carried from Buffalo to New York for even less than one cent per bushel. We have to face that state of affairs. Besides our great rival, the Mr. TARTE.
Erie canal, we have to reckon with the Mississippi and the Missouri and the Gulf of Mexico routes. Unless we take good care to handle our Canadian transportation policy in the right way, these rivals will certainly take away from us the trade of the Canadian Northwest that we have a right to expect.

I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) to take the facts as his best guide. My hon. friend should not forget that Sir Sandford Fleming advocates a line further north, and not the location proposed

by the government for this line. But auj^-way, what are the facts ? I have here the report of the New York ' Produce Exchange,' and that shows that during the season of navigation the rates are low and when the season of navigation closes up go the rates. At Minneapolis, St. Paul, Chicago, Buffalo and Duluth, the Americans have erected immense elevators in which to store grain, pending the opening of navigation. Every one knows that only a small quantity of grain is carried in the winter months, and that for local milling purposes, very little for export. Sir Sandford Fleming's words are very respectable, but the facts are against him, the practice of all the railway companies is against him. The Grand Trunk itself have a large fleet on the lakes ; hundreds of boats plied last year between Sarnia and American ports ; all the railway companies follow the same policy. Mr. Booth, of the Canada Atlantic, has three American registered vessels and two Canadian registered, he has his agents at all lake points, and carries grain and general cargo to Parry Sound, sending it over his short piece of railway to Coteau and Montreal. He would adopt other means if it were more profitable for him to do so. The opinion or Sir Sand-ford Fleming is very respectable, but I would venture to say that there are not two other railway engineers on the continent who share it.
Mr. MeCREARY. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) has stated that the Grand Trunk would not require to use this road from Winnipeg to Quebec, because they can secure a road very cheaply from Winnipeg to Duluth and from Duluth to Ashland and secure the Wisconsin Central from Ashland to Chicago. He says that you can build a railway from Winnipeg to Duluth in 360 miles, but my opinion is that it will be more like 460 miles. Anyhow do you suppose the Wisconsin Central is going to sell a small piece of their road to the Grand Trunk Railway unless they take the whole road and its terminals? I do not think so. It is stated now that Mr. Rockfeller has purchased the Wisconsin Central, or has an option on it. The Grand Trunk were supposed to have an opinion on it but that option has expired. But even suppose the Grand Trunk could reach Chicago as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) states, then if that were the cheapest way to carry the grain of the Northwest, why in the name of Heaven should these business men of the Grand Trunk come here and ask the government to give them a road from North Bay to Winnipeg ? It is much easier to construct a railway from North Bay to Quebec, than it is from North Bay to Winnipeg.

How do you know ?
Mr. MeCREARY. I believe any engineer will say so. I make that statement, just the same as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte)
- 804
made his statement; I make the statement because I have been informed that it is much more difficult to build from a point north of Lake Nipigon and thence to Winnipeg, than it is to build a road from a point north of North Bay to Quebec. And yet these people, who according to the hon. member (Mr. Tarte) could have got to Chicago by Duluth and the Wisconsin Central, came to this government and asked for a charter from North Bay to Winnipeg and guaranteed to make it pay. If they could make that pay they could make the road to Quebec pay very much better, because they have to haul from North Bay to Portland

	.

On a line which is alreadv built.
Mr. MeCREARY. But they have to pay the interest on the bonds of that line.

Certainly ; it will help them to pay the interest.
Mr. MeCREARY. They will have to pay the interest on the cost of that road just the same as they will have to pay the interest on the cost of the road from North Bay to Quebec.

Are they bound to-day to build that part of the line ?
Mr. MeOREARY. If they had asked for a charter from the Dominion parliament and got a subsidy, I suppose they would have been bound to do it.. It was stated the other day that they got only $3,200 a mile. I think there is evidence that they asked more subsidy for that road than would build it to-day. The hon. gentleman talks about carrying grain by water. We all admit that grain can be carried by water at a lower rate than by rail or by rail and water. At the same time a great deal more than the difference may be lost by the grain lying idle. A farmer's binder may be used only three or four weeks in the year, yet he has to pay interest on it all the year round. It may surprise the hon. gentleman to know that there are still this season 15,000,000 bushels of wheat in elevators and in the farmers' hands west of Lake Superior ; I have a report from the warehouse commissioner to that effect. What does it cost to hold that wheat over from the close of navigation, say the 1st of December, to the end of May 1 That would put the grain into seven terms of storage at f cent per bushel per term, or a total cost for storage and insurance of 5J cents per bushel ; and if you value that wheat at an a verage of 80 cents per bushel, the bank interest on 1,000 bushels at 6 per cent would add another $4 per month to the cost of the wheat, which would bring the total carrying charges per month to 1 -15 cents per bushel, or, for the six months, the total charge for storage, insurance and bank interest is say 6'90 cents per bushel. Now, the freight rates by the Canadian Pacific Railway last
.2510

winter on grain to west St. John for export were 22J cents per 100 pounds, or 13J cents per bushel, whereas the water rate from Fort William and Tort Arthur to Montreal is from 5 to 5J cents per bushel. This rate fluctuates from time to time. For instance, there may be held at Superior and Duluth from 10,000,000 to 15,000,000 bushels, and the vessels that wintered there might carrs-that wheat ou their lirst trip at as low as 1J cents per bushel. Thus the shipper who is compelled to carry his grain over in store until he can ship it out by water to Montreal only effects a saving of about li cents per bushel over what it would cost him if he shipped by all-rail to St. John, and it is interesting to any one who has studied these matters to note how' closely the all-rail rate to St. John and the winter storage charges added to the lake rates to Montreal agree. My friend who gives me this information remarks :
It is unnecessary to point out to you who so thoroughly understand the requirements of all western interests how essentially important it is to bend every effort to remove from the back of the farmer this heavy winter-carrying charge of nearly 8 cents per bushel, and in these competitive times it is a burden he should not he asked to carry.
The farmer has that much surplus to com? and go upon if he wants his wheat carried by all-rail. I do not say that the railway can compete during the summer ; but in winter, as the box cars are there, why not use them ? They will certainly pay expenses. Then, what about the merchandise coming west V I mentioned the other day that one train had arrived at Winnipeg two weeks ago last Saturday which was the heaviest train that ever went to the west. It had 83 cars loaded with manufactured goods from the east. When these goods are delivered, what will the railway do with the empties ? All these cars will be empty in two weeks. The navigation on the lakes is not yet open, and these cars will have to run back empty. I say that these box cars could bring back wheat at a rate that would pay the farmers better than to leave their wheat in store all winter, paying charges for storage, insurance and bank interest. 1 will put any member of the grain exchange of Winnipeg on evidence before the Committee on Agriculture, and I believe that he will prove that to he the case.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte), and t think his solution of the transportation question is the correct one. At least it agrees with the opinion I have formed. He made the statement that for nearly seven months of the year transportation by water from the head of Lake Superior to the ocean is the solution of the problem. I wi's venture to say that the consensus of opinion among railroad men in the country is that no road built either north or south of Lake
Mr. .McCreary.
Superior can compete in the summer months with the water communication of the St. Lawrence. Then, what is our duty in the matter ? Our duty is to see that the canal system and the water-ways from the head of Lake Superior to the ocean are made as perfect as possible. As I have stated again and again in this House, nature has placed this country at an advantage over the neighbouring country to the south of us in regard to transportation. By means of the St. Lawrence and the lakes we have the control of freights to the seaport from the head of Lake Superior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What should be done with the canals ?

The right hon. gentleman evidently was not in the House when I made a speech on that question, in which I explained fully what ought to be done We have 20-foot navigation down to Port Colborne. I think that ought to he extended by building another canal past Niagara Falls. That would give us 20-foot navigation to Prescott. To carry it from Prescott to Montreal would require an expenditure which we, perhaps, would not be justified in making at present. At any rate, the expenditure required for this would build what, in my opinion, is the best solution of the question-a 20-foot navigation by the Ottawa river and the Georgian Bay canal to Montreal. Then, as I have stated before, we ought to see that the facilities at the port of Montreal are the best. We ought to see that the navigation from Montreal to Quebec is made so safe that a boat could pass by night or day between these two ports without the slightest danger. That could be done by ndoptiug the system which the Americans have adopted at Hay lake below the St. Mary's river, where the channel into Lake Michigan is so well lighted by electricity that there is no more danger to vessels during the night than there is during the day.
Notwithstanding the statement of Sir Sandford Fleming or of any other gentleman, I here state that the consensus of opinion among all parties interested in the transportation question is that during the season of navigation no railway can compete successfully with water communication. My right lion, friend criticised the opposition for granting a charter to the Grand Trunk Railway, but my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte), was not objecting to tbe Grand Trunk Railway getting into tbe Northwest. What he said was this: you are building a railway from Winnipeg to Quebec and giving it to the Grand Trunk Railway, what object has the Grand Trunk Railway io carry freight from Winnipeg to Quebec ? And my hon. friend pointed out that the Grand Trunk Railway could secure a road from Winnipeg to Duluth, thence to Ashland and Chicago and thence to Portland, and the interest on the expenditure involved would be a million dollars a year less

than they would have to pay the government for this road which the government are to build. What object, then, have they to go to Quebec? That was the argument of my hon. friend. Then the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) asked: why is it, if they intended to utilize that road, that they should ask a charter to build a line to the head of Lake Superior? Evidently the reason is that if they had a road built to Chicago, and a rival line had the railway to Quebec, the Grand Trunk Railway would have to compete with the other line in carrying grain to the seaboard and would require to have some means of carrying it as cheaply. The only possible way would be to get to the head of Lake Superior as quickly as possible, put the grain on boai'd their boats, carry it to Midland. and thence over their own line to Portland.
My hon. friend objects also to our placing the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the hands of a company whose interests, financially and every other way will lead it to carry the freight over its own line to Portland. However, 1 am strongly of the opinion that if we consider the opportunities given us by nature and otherwise, we would find that the cheapest line of transport is through our own country, and that if we take proper advantage of our opportunities, we will be able to command the immense trade which must be developed in the Northwest and Manitoba. There are three ways in which that trade may go to the ocean. Mr. Hays in his address to the Grand Trunk Railway shareholders, said that the day is not far distant when there will be a greater quantity of grain carried to the Pacific coast than to Lake Superior. The parties who control the Canadian Northern Railway think t that the solution of the transportation question, as far as Manitoba and the Northwest are concerned, is to get to Hudson Bay, and they intend to build a line to that point. They are in earnest. They believe that the greater portion of the surplus grain of that immense region will find a market in Europe, not by Lake Superior, but by Hudson Bay. Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann are at present contemplating the building of a line to Fort Churchill and building large elevators there, and are interesting parties iii Great Britain to build receiving elevators there. They say that they can solve the question of feeding the British empire with all the cereals at command by facilitating transportation by Hudson Bay. But the people of the eastern section are interested in making the transport to our section of the country as cheap as possible. We say that nature intended we should stick as closely as possible to our water-ways. The right hon. gentleman read an extract from Sir Sandford Fleming's opinions to prove that railways built on
modern principles-that is, with four-tenths of a foot per hundred-can compete with water-ways. Well, four-tenths of a foot per hundred means virtually a level road, because a locomotive will draw on a four-tenths grade just as much as on the level.
Not at all.

1 say yes, and I can give authority for the statement. The reason is simply this, that to start a locomotive at a station requires as much power as when it is in motion to carry it over a four-tenths grade. Read any engineering authority. Read the ' Scientific American.' Like my hon. friend, X used to have some doubts as to the reason, but the reason is sound, and there is no object whatever in having a railway level, because a four-tenths per cent grade is practically the same as a level road. To obtain that grade from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton, does my right hon. friend contemplate what the cost will be? To make a 26-foot grade going easterly, and even doubling the amount goiifg westerly, would entail an expenditure of $50,000 per mile. To reduce the gradients to a four-tenths per cent would require an expenditure of nearly $80,000 per mile. Are the people prepared for any such expenditure? I have always been in favour of developing the Northwest by railway communication. My idea has always been that the starting point should be North Bay or Lake Superior, and go north of Lake Winnipeg, and I was glad to see that a company with the enterprise of the Grand Trunk were interesting themselves in this. I believe that that company has done a great deal for the benefit of this country, and if any assistance be given to any railway at all, it is perfectly justifiable that the government should give it to that railway. But I have always objected to the expenditure of money for a road which I believe is entirely useless, and which I believe now will never be built. I never could understand any argument in favour of building a road from Quebec to Moncton. The argument in favour of a road from Quebec to North Bay is that it may develop that portion of the country. As the right hon. gentleman says, there may be in that country many waterfalls, from which electricity may be developed, and there may be mineral and timber resources, but before we spend money on a railway, we should have accurate surveys. We should have some knowledge of the country. We should know whether it possesses anything of the kind, and in the first instance we should develop it by a cheap colonization road, and not waste the resources of the country in useless extravagance.
Let us return now to the question before the chair, namely, the issue of stock to the
.2523

Grand Trunk Pacific. Let us see the position of the Grand Trunk Railway with regard to this enterprise. They go security for the building of one-quarter of the road from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. That gives the Grand Trunk Railway no monetary interest in the undertaking except this, that, should the undertaking not pay sufficiently to meet the interest on that quarter section, they will be liable for it. Of what benefit, then, to the Grand Trunk Railway will be the building of this particular portion? Under the Act of last year, it is provided that $45,000,000 of stock may be issued, of which it was obligatory on the Grand Trunk to own $25,000,000. That gave them a vested interest in the road. That gave to the Grand Trunk Railway, if ever the undertaking was a paying ope, over and above the interest payable on the bonds, rolling stock and working expenses, an interest in the road. I can understand how the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are interested in the undertaking, for they have to operate the road. But, this bargain gives to the Grand Trunk Railway Company power to acquire the whole $45,000,000 of stock, the only obligation being that they shall hold a majority of the said stock by such title as shall enable the Grand Trunk Railway Company to control the policy of the company. The Grand Trunk Railway Company need not own one dollar's worth of stock, all they have to do is to control a majority so as to direct the policy of the company. Hon. members may ask how they can do that without holding the stock. It is done every day in reference to railways. The right to vote, the power to control the franchise, may be vested in one individual -and the stock in another.
How can that be done V Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) please explain the process ?

It is done every day. You get permanent power of attorney to exercise the right of voting on the stock. It is done in the United States in many instances so as to give the voting power to parties who have not invested a dollar in the stock.
The hon. gentleman says that, in the sale of stock this follows as a matter of course, or does he say that it can be arranged ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, it can be arranged ?	,

And it is done every day. A man can buy the stock, and yet the power to vote on it may remain with the vendor. I do not know whether the stock is absolutely transferred or whether it is only for a number of years-fifty or ninety-nine years

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is it legal ;

Yes, it is legal in the United States and it would be here. What do the government contemplate by this section if not some such condition as this ? Here is the whole section :-
% 9- Notwithstanding anything in the twenty-seventh paragraph of the said contract contained, the Grand Trunk Railway [DOT] Company shall not, after the acquisition of the twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) of common stock therein mentioned (less shares held by directors, not exceeding one thousand), he prevented from making any such disposition of such common stock as the Grand Trunk Railway may deem expedient, provided, however, that the said Grand Trunk Railway Company shall, during the delay mentioned in the said paragraph, continue to hold a majority of the said stock by such title as shall enable the said Grand Trunk Railway Company to control the policy of the company.
It is not ownership at all, but simply to hold it by such title as shall enable them to control the policy. Now, what interest has the Grand Trunk Railway in the undertaking ? They may part with the whole of the stock and not have even an estate in expectancy in it-they may not expect that the stock will be returned to them in any way. They have only this, which may be indirectly profitable to them-they control the policy of the road and may make such arrangements as may be of benefit to themselves. . I cannot understand and have never been able to understand the argument of the Minister of Finance In reference to this question of stock. You issue certain securities which you call stock and you issue certain other securities which you call bonds or debentures. And they become complicated at once. But here is the simplest kind of a proposition. You provide for the issue of $45,000,000 of stock as to the majority of which the Grand Trunk Railway Company is to bold the voting power on a majority. But they may absolutely dispose of the stock itself. Then, what interest has the Grand Trunk Company in the road ? Their only interest is that they are liable for one-quarter of the cost of construction-for which they have first-class security-pari passu with the government, on the whole undertaking

	'
On the Grand Trunk Pacific only.

On the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the coast. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would control the policy of the company and that it would be liable for three per cent on the value of the eastern division. The Grand Trunk Railway Company are not liable for a single dollar of the interest. The contract with reference to that is made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The liability of the Grand Trunk Railway Company is that described

by the president of the road to his stockholders ; and the whole liability of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in reference to this undertaking is simply one quarter of the cost of the line from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And merely a guarantee at that.

And merely a guarantee at that. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) may say that we have the promise from the Grand Trunk Railway Company that they shall hold the majority of the stock so as to control the policy of the company. In what way is he going to enforce that ? Will he apply to the courts to compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company to retain such a hold upon the stock as to enable them to control the policy of this company ? There may be some legal process by which it can be done, but I do not know what it can be. There are no penalties under this Act, and if penalties are provided anywhere, I would like to know what they are. So, that is the position-the Grand Trunk Railway Company are liable for one-quarter of the cost of construction of the western division and no further. The interest that they have in the undertaking is not given to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but, if I may call them so, to the speculators who constitute the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Under the original contract, they had only a half interest in the undertaking, but now you give them absolute control. All the stock may be in other hands, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company may receive no benefit from the whole proposition except that they control the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific. And, if I calculate rightly that will be just as long as the Grand Trunk Railway Company see that it is to their interest to do so. '

We hear a great deal of discussion over the clauses about the stock of this company and about the policy being controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. And the government would give us to understand that to keep the Grand Trunk Railway Company in control is to the interest of the people of Canada. One would naturally suppose that the Grand Trunk people in securing that control would be looking for the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Now, we have the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) here. And, as I have been studying up the views of that hon. gentleman, and as the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) does not seem at all confident of the views of his colleague, I shall endeavour while we are upon this aspect of the case, to give to the Prime Minister and to the House the views that I have learned from the utterances of the Minister of Railways and Canals, whose voice is singularly silent upon this great question. Now.
the Grand Trunk Railway Company is to control the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Pacific western division, extending from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast is to be constructed on the guarantee of three-fourths by the government and one-fourth by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. And the people of Canada are to build, I presume under Grand Trunk supervision, the road from Winnipeg to North Bay line, from the North Bay line to Quebec, and from Quebec to Moncton.
The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are not obliged to take over one mile of the government road, not even by agreement, until every foot of it is completed to Moncton. Am I right or wrong ? If the company choose to take over any constructed portion of the road east of Winnipeg, they may do so, but upon conditions which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company lay down. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company control the stock of its own road, and control the entire read from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The Grand Trunk controls the Grand Trunk Pacific. Does any one suppose that the Grand Trunk are going to manage the Grand Trunk Pacific to the detriment of the Grand Trunk. If they do, I must say that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays and the gentlemen associated with them are not the business men that the people of this country took them to be. The Prime Minister made a very important admission to-night. If we keep on we will have important admissions all along the line. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) made one last night when he said that the government were obliged to do so and so by the Grand Trunk. In reading this matter [DOT] up from start to finish and examining it in all its features, we find that the whole business has been dictated by the Grand Trunk Railway. We cannot accuse the gigantic intellect of the present Minister' of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) of evolving this scheme. We certainly cannot accuse the late Minister of Railways of doing so, and judging by the half-hearted support of members of the government and the blank faces of their supporters, the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior are alone responsible for this agreement. I believe the Prime Minister has been carried awa.v with the notion of a great transcontinental railway. Why did he not follow the policy of the Minister of Railways and the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) and those who were behind them in reference to this ? We will come down to the question of control of this railway and I want to say, if the government is honest, as I believe they are, if the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is honest-although the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) said that they were-not honest in any undertaking they ever made-if the government, if these people who govern the Grand Trunk and the Grand.

Trunk Pacific, are all honest in this matter, the company should be ready to give a guarantee to the country for the faithful execution of this contract. The Prime Minister said a moment ago that there was r. penalty. I searched in vain in the agreement, in the amended agreement, in the contract, and in the charter, for any penalty direct or indirect, upon the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific for non-operation of this road from Winnipeg east. He said that the whole stock of the company would be a penalty for the non-carrying out of the contract in relation to the eastern division. I trust the Prime Minister will look it up as lie promised and have it. ready and be aide to show the House and the country where it comes in. It has not been shown yet, and his skilled Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton), who made a very able speech on this matter, has not pointed this out. How does the matter stand ? T.et us take for purposes of illustration in a concrete form, two carloads of freight which start from the Pacific coast and come down across the continent. They come to Winnipeg over the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Pacific, of course, will get all the freight arising from that traffic. Once it gets to Winnipeg on this new line, wii! the Prime Minister be good enough to point out to me whether the Grand Trunk Rail-nay Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is going to be benefited by that freight over the Eastern Division. I have looked in vain, I have asked in vain, for an answer. On the other band, supposing that the policy that has been outlined so ably to-night by the member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Mr. Tarte), a policy which I had the honour of pointing out to this House last year, and which every one who knows anything about the matter knows is the true policy of the Grand Trunk is carried out in regard to one car. They have their connection south through Minneapolis as their main line with a branch to Duluth, and connect with the present Grand Trunk system at Chicago, on the .way to Portland and Boston. Supposing that policy is carried out in relation to one car and then let us contrast the two. The two cars of freight go from the Pacific to Winnipeg, one deviates south from Winnipeg and goes over the Grand Trunk via Chicago to Portland. Supposing the charges on that car are $3(30, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk will get every dollar of that freight, and they are not paying three per cent interest on their line, they have to maintain the line through the United States, and are under no burden ; they owe allegience only to their stockholders. The other car proceeds to Moncton and on to some Canadian port, Halifax or St. John. The whole $360 of that freight does not go to the Grand Trunk Pacific ; part if Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
it has to go in paying the indebtedness of 3 per cent on the cost of this government section, and the balance of it, for the haul only as far as Winnipeg, say $160, goes to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Does any on-1 suppose that the Grand Trunk stockholders, who control the Grand Trunk directors, who control the Grand Trunk Pacific, are going to permit that state of affairs to continue and have their road and their terminals at Portland lose this traffic ? I am satisfied that the Grand Trunk shareholders will rot permit any such state of affairs to exist for one instant. We have the statement made by the Minister of the Interior, in his speech as to the obligation of the company. He says that we have the obligation that they are to make a deposit of $5,000,000. But he himself goes on and points out that after all, that is no obligation, for it is paid back to tlie company, and it is only a question of financing. The minister says the money does not have in be ultimately provided. Tlie next obligation he points out, has less in it even than that. The next obligation is to build the western section of the railway, and for the purpose of doing this, they have first the government" bonds for tliree-quarters and then their own bonds for one-quarter of the cost. This will dispose of the original construction of the railway. Tt e obligation of the Grand Trunk in regard +n this is practically nothing. The Grand Trunk guarantees one-quarter and the gov-eminent the other three-quarters of the cost of construction and the rolling stock is provided by another clause, and has been pointed out by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), will lie controlled by a rolling stock trust. Thus that obligation falls to the ground. By the third obligation he says they are obliged to lease and operate the eastern section and pay the rental. I want the Prime Minister to be good enough to point out wherein they are obliged to lease and operate the eastern section aud pay the rental ? I grant that ic is in the agreement, but only when every mile is built from Winnipeg to Moncton. If that line is one mile short of Moncton, the contract falls. I am satisfied there is not one member of this parliament and I very much doubt if the grandsons of the members who are sitting in this parliament will be in existence when that road is completed all the way from Winnipeg to Moncton. Therefore, until that hour arrives the contract does not begin to have effect, and in the meantime any part of the road which is finished may be taken over by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon their own terms. Even though the road is constructed, I want the right hon. Prime Minister to point out any penalty which will be invoked as against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in the event that they refuse, as I think they will refuse, to take charge of that road. I want to see

where the penalty is by which we can com- | pel the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to turn one wheel on that road in case they do not consider it to be in their in terest to do so. The next obligation is to equip the road with rolling stock to the value of 820,000,000. That has been reduced to $15,000,000 in the new agreement, and, as has been pointed out, there is no obligation whatever on the part of the Grand Trunk raeific Railway Company, or of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, because they will simply give a mortgage to a rolling stock trust. The next one is that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall induce and procure the Grand Trunk Railway Company to guarantee the second mortgage bonds on the rolling stock. As I pointed out, that rolling stock will be controlled by a rolling stock trust, and although it may be included in the agreement it is really ultra vires of the agreement. The next one is that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall enter into an obligation to carry their freight through Canadian channels and give as good a rate by the Canadian route as is given by the United States route. These are all the obligations that even the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) can conjure up that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company are under to the people of Canada. Now, to sustain these obligations there is not the value of a farthing in case the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Railway Company default in their agreement. To show that I am justified in coming to this conclusion, I shall quote the [DOT]words of wisdom uttered by the present hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Em merson). It is true that when he uttered these words of wisdom he was not tied up by the iron hand of the right hon. Prime Minister. He was not under an obligation to sacrifice his will and to bend his genius to that of the right hon. Prime Minister. He was a very independent member of parliament. When this debate was going on during last session the question arose as to the route and as to the general policy in connection with the construction of the road. The present hon. Minister of Railways and Canals then said :
I say that the government of Canada is not prepared and the people of Canada will not sustain them in at once immediately subsidizing a road south of Lake Winnipeg. (Hear, hear.) I say that the necessities of this country do not demand it.
A little later on, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston), who said :
"You are discussing the matter of a charter now.
He said :
Precisely, I am discussing the matter of a charter, and I say that this committee should not place the government in the position, or
permit any government if it would do it, to be placed in the position whereby they could subsidize a line south of Winnipeg at this stage of the history of Canada. (Hear, hear.) Now that is the position which I take. I take another position. I say that we should not incorporate any body of men. I have nothing to say against the gentlemen whose names appear in this first section, but I say that the parliament of Canada is not qualified in giving such rights to any man at this time with the possibility, no probability, that it would be followed by large government assistance.
These are the words of the present hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. I do not know whether the right hon. Prime Minister heard them. I know they will have no effect whatever upon the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), because the hon. Minister of Agriculture Is known to have no opinion upon anything. But I would like if the right hon. Prime Minister would be good enough to listen to the words of his own Minister of Railways and Canals. He has been so impressed with the views of his late Minister of Railways and Canals that he now considers him as the first railway expert on the continent of America, if not in the universe. Possibly the words of wisdom that I am quoting from the present hon. Minister of Railways and Canals may influence the right hon. Prime Minister yet. and before this session ends we will see him rise and withdraw this Bill in order that it may he further amended. If he does he will have our endorsation. There will be no division upon that question. Now, the present lion. Minister of Railways and Canals went further, and. speaking from the same subject, said :
But on the other hand, if you subsidize the railway, if you subsidize only one now, you would haVe a large indebtedness, but wherein are you going to have the benefit ? Wherein do you have the returns ?
The people would benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Certainly, I grant you that. You subsidize the roads and the people get the benefit ; I am willing to admit' that, but if you take the same amount of money and construct a road, instead of giving a subsidy, you have an asset for [DOT]your expenditure. You do not have that when you pay that money out in the way of subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I am delighted that the hou. Minister of Railways and Canals adheres to his convictions. Following out the principle of the joint responsibility of the cabinet, he must either stand by his convictions or go back upon them, and if he does stand by his convictions he must get out of the cabinet. If he gets out of the cabinet we will have another exhibition of a Minister of Railways and Canals leaving the cabinet in justification of what he believes ought to be the government's policy. I would like the right hon. Prime Minister to listen to this particularly. I would like

even the hon. Minister of Agriculture, if be can grasp the idea, to listen to it:
You may put in this charter, or add to it a clause which you may think would guarantee to the people of Canada an ail-rail route over Canadian soil, and guarantee that the exports shall go through Canadian ports, but you will not accomplish what you propose to do.
These are some of the opinions of the present hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, and we want him to stand up in this House, because we want to see if he has lost his voice on this subject, and tell the people whether he has changed his views or whether he still adheres to his views, and, if so, why he still retains his position in the government. He goes on to say :
