It will be evaded at every point, and it seems to me that the gentlemen who are promoting this Bill gave evidence of it at every turn, that they do not consider and have not taken into consideration the proposal that the products of Canada shall be shipped over an alternating line, through Canadian seaports ; they have not it in their minds, the history of the Bill, the remarks of the hon. president of the company, gave evidence of that in every sentence which he uttered.
Let me add that every sentence which has been uttered by the president or manager of the company since, and the whole conduct of the negotiations from that day to this, carry out the words of wisdom uttered by this simple-I mean simple in the honest sense of the term-honest member for Westmoreland. I do not know whether it is advisable to quote that hon. gentleman still further or not, but he says :
I say and I am impressed beyond measure with the idea that you cannot carry out any suggestion contained herein and guarantee to the people of Canada what we all would like to see. And the only other alternative is by the government constructing a line of railway over the shortest route and having control over the rates.
Then he goes on to say :
But I say attempt as much as you will, exercise your endeavours with all the acumen with which you may, you will not control to the people of Canada their seaport with an allCanadian route.
These are the words of the member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) now the Minister of Railways. He goes on :

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The point is this. Do you want to help western people get their grain to the sea-board ? Do we want to help them to get it to a Canadian seaport ? Do we want to help them get it there over an all-Canadian line ?
And do we want to make our help effective ?
Well, then, I say that the only way you can do it is by demanding and insisting upon the carrying out of the idea, the extension of the government owned road across this continent. (Hear, hear.)

Such are the views of the present Minister of Railways and Canals. I regard the control of this stock as a guarantee that the Grand Trunk interest first, the Grand Trunk Pacific interest second, and the interest of the people last, are going to be looked after. If these private negotiations are ever made public, I venture to say it will be found that the Grand Trunk people insisted upon these clauses being placed in the contract so that they might control not only the Grand Trunk Railway interest, but corner the entire freight for their own system and render the whole government road nugatory. There is another feature of this : the Ontario government have given a cash subsidy per mile, and also a subsidy of 6,400 acres of land per mile, to a branch of this road to Lake Superior.
Surely not a Reform government.

Oh, yes, a Reform government did it; although they are opposed to land subsidies, they swallow their principles to suit the occasion. The1 Prime Minister has been exercised to make it appear that he is bent upon having a Canadian port on Lake Superior, instead of Duluth. In his own province of Quebec his name, rightly or wrongly, has more or less of magic in it, and his name carries more weight there than it does where his policy is understood ; but he found that even the people of Quebec demanded a Canadian port. The Prime Minister himself has admitted to-night-it is one of the secrets that has leaked out-that it was the original policy of the Grand Trunk to come south of Lake Superior, and that they had the hardihood to propose that to him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To propose what to me ?
Mi-. SAM. HUGHES. The Prime Minister admitted to-night that the Grand Trunk Company first proposed to go south of Lake Superior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I admitted nothing of the kind.
Certainly ; the first minister said south of Lake Superior, and I said south of Lake Winnipeg ; and he repeated it and said : south of Lake Superior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I made no such admission, and I do not- think ' Hansard ' will verify the hon. gentleman's statement. At all events, I never intended to make any such statement, because there is no truth in it.

I thought the First Minister meant north of Lake Winnipeg.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, North of Lake Superior.

I interrupted by interjecting the words, 'Lake Winnipeg' and

the Prime Minister said the first proposition was to come south of Lake Superior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
I venture to say that Hansard will bear me out. I am neither deaf nor blind, and I interrupted the first minister because I thought he was making a mistake.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I certainly would have made a mistake had I said that.
The Prime Minister admitted that the first proposition was that they should go south of Lake Superior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no.
The ' Hansard ' will show who is right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, if I did say it, it was a slip of the tongue. There was never such a proposition made to us.
The right hon. gentleman was referring to the remarks made by the member for St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte), and that is how he came to refer to the south of Lake Superior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps so.
Well, anyway 1 know it was the first proposition of the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not want to contradict my hon, friend any more, but if he wants to say that we received from the Grand Trunk Railway Company any proposition to asist a line south of Lake Superior, he is all wrong.

The first proposition was not made by the company because it was not then organized as a company, but the first proposition was that there should be an extension of the Grand Trunk Railway from Chicago, through to Minneapolis and Winnipeg, and on to the coast. I know it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But it is not so.

I know it was the proposition, and I have every reason to believe that it was submitted to the government, and then it was pointed out that the country would not endorse it, and that they must come to North Bay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No such thing.
I know that the first charter was asked to North Bay, but the negotiations before that were for an American road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Never.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Never.

Why, the Quebec bridge had not commenced to dawn on the
people at that time, and my hon. friend was asleep until he saw the possibility of extending the line from North Bay to Quebec. The Minister of Justice then became interested, and said we must force this on to Quebec, and then the gentleman from the maritime provinces took the thing up, and said it must be continued to Moncton.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are very few people who pay much attention to the wild statements made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes). Perhaps he thinks that in order to be forcible and interesting he must be insulting and impertinent, and that is what he is now.

There is nothing insulting about it. Every one knows that the Minister of Justice took no interest in that Bill until he suddenly saw it could go to Quebec, and then he woke up on the stage of the Railway Committee room and in this House. He knows it, and he cannot by any little bit of an exhibition of his Hibernian temper alter the facts. He will understand that the people of this country can size him up as far as they can see him. The whole business from start to finish shows that this government has been dictated to, and that they rushed into this without consulting even their colleagues in the cabinet, or the members behind them, much less the parliament and the people of Canada. The whole matter has been forced on by one or two men in the cabinet to the detriment of the people of Canada. If the people of the country are not appealed to before this Bill becomes law, then when they are appealed to and in case the verdict of the people should be against it; despite any efforts that may be made to the contrary, every contract gotten and given under this charter and under this legislation will be cancelled in the interests of the people of Canada. I would be delighted now, and I am sure the whole House and the country would be delighted, to hear the Minister of Railways give his views on this subject.

Having spoken last year on the general proposition, but I did not intend to say anything in connection with the Bill this session ; but so many statements have been made, coming from such eminent authority, that it almost seems necessary for some one who has got the cheek to get up and dispute the correctness of these statements made by gentlemen on the other side. I heard to-night, with what confidence and with what assurance the late Minister of Railways made the statement, that a railway of four-tenths grade is equal in capacity to a practically level road. When the ex-Minister of Railways makes a statement like that, with so much confidence, one should scrutinize almost afraid to dispute the accuracy of this assertion. But I have under my hand the Canadian Pacific Railway standards with respect to the grades of

[DOT]2530
railways, and also the standards of Mr. Wel-'ington, and these statements are diametrically opposed to the statements made hy the ex-Minister of Railways.
Every statement that he makes with that degree of assurance and confidence must be just as carefully scrutinized as the statement he made to-night with respect to the gradients of the railway. He stated that a four-tenths grade railway was equal to a level road. What does Mr. Wellington say in his table ? He says that an engine with an 18-inch by 24-inch cylinder is capable on the level, of drawing 2,183 tons, while on a four-tenths grade it is capable of drawing 1,058 tons, or just about cne-half. Yet the lion. ex-Minister of Railways has the assurance to try to force it down the throats of the members of this House that a four-tenths grade railway is practically equal to a level railway; and when I dared to question the statement, he said, who denies this? I said I did. Of course, I did not of my own knowledge, but I had the statement in my hand which proved the incorrectness of the hon. gentleman's statement. The Canadian Pacific Railway tables say the same engine is capable of drawing 1,500 tons on a one-tentli grade, or 1,200 tons on a four-tenths grade. So the statements of 'the Canadian Pacific Railway authorities and Mr. Wellington are diametrically opposed to the statement made by the ex-Minister of Railways. Therefore when one of the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House gives his opinion or makes a statement, it is necessary to make a careful examination to ascertain whether it is really true, and I am in the habit of verifying the correctness of a great many of their statements. Now, if everything the hon. gentleman has said in regard to that railway is no more truthful than his remarks as to the equality of the gradients, they are entirely unworthy of consideration. I was very much interested in the remarks made by my hon. friend the late Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tartel. He speaks with such a degree of assurance and of confidence as to almost convince one that he tnorouglily understands the subject about which he is talking? I am willing to admit that he has had opportunities of acquainting himself with these matters; but with all respect to the good qualities of my hon. friend, his mind is not logically inclined, and he is often apt to dwell in the realms of imagination.

You found that out very late.
Mr. HEY'D. Oh, you are all right. When I ventured to ask him how he harmonized his statements with the opinions of one whom he esteems and respects, he did not say that Sir Sandford Fleming was an old lady, but he did not exactly accept as correct the statements which that gentleman Mr. HEYD.	'
has made. I think that an opinion expressed by Sir Sandford Fleming is entitled to serious consideration, because he has had years of experience, and any statement he makes we are always satisfied is made with the honest intention of informing the general public. In addition to the statement I have read, he went on further to say:
A railway constructed on the northern route would, at all times and seasons, be a reliable outlet from the granary of the empire in the heart of Canada to tide-water. Moreover, at Quebec in summer, and at the open ports of the maritime provinces in winter, the ships transporting produce to Great Britain would, when necessary, he placed under the express protection of the British fleet.
Such a railway constructed between Quebec and the western prairies on the northern route would be a national highway in every sense. Its immediate effect would be to broaden the Dominion, to add strength where strength is so much needed, to establish many new centres of industry, and thus the country would steadily become populated and consolidated. What is now a widespread wilderness would be converted into one of the most important divisions of the Dominion.
1 am quite willing to confess that the opinion expressed by Sir Sandford Fleming has considerable weight with me.
Not on this scheme. Eet my hon. friend be frank.

Would the hon. gentleman allow me to put him a question ? Does he know that the statement of the hon. member for North Norfolk, based upon a letter of Mr. Scott, was that one dollar was the cost of a train mile on the Grand Trunk Railway, and that he overlooked how many cars were contained in the average train of the Grand Trunk Railway on which the dollar was based, and multiplied it by nearly four in order to deduce an argument as to what he could work on the northern line for ?
I remember perfectly well my' hon. friend's reply. Bet me point out that Mr. Ledyard also was quoted in a letter which he wrote in respect to the Canadian Southern.
Who is he ?

President of the Michigan Central. The Canada Southern road is of a three-tenths grade, and on that railway they carry 2,400 tons, or nearly 80,000 bushels, to the train mile, and the average cost in 1892 was 81.1(1 per mile and $1.60 in 1903.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent. The train mileage of $1.16 is the average of all their trains. Some have only four and some have forty cars. It is the average of the lot. The hon. gentleman applies that to a six-car train or a fifty-car train, as if you could apply the cost of hauling the average, say' of fifteen cars, to a train of fifty or sixty !

I heard the hon. gentleman's argument last year, and gave a great deal of attention. The Grand Trunk Railway7 train mileage costs 9S cents ; the Canada Atlantic, 91 cents ; the Canadian Pacific Railway', $1.11 and last year $1.23 ; and the cost of the government road per train mile was 92 cents. That was the average train mileage, including passenger trains and freight. There are large trains and small trains, and we have a right now to begin to approximate, and to that extent the argument I intend to present may be attacked. What train mileage will it be fair to apply on the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to Quebec over such a road as the government intend to build ? If it is a four-tenths grade road, it is capable of hauling with one engine of the same power a load three times as large as that of almost any road in Canada, except the Canada Southern. That is one of the facts which must be taken into consideration. Therefore, for the purposes of argument. I have assumed that the inside cost will be $1.60 per train mile. If that is not a fair margin, to the extent to which it is not fair, my argument will be incorrect, but assuming that $1.60 per mile is correct, then this railway could haul grain from Winnipeg to Quebec under the following

conditions : Assuming the haul over a four-tenths grade road would be 40,000 bushels per train, and taking the freight rate of 12 cents per bushel from Winnipeg to Quebec, you have a gross receipt from that train of $4,200.
The assumption is all wrong.

It is a matter of multiplication. A train capable of hauling 40,000 bushels, which an engine and the gradients of our road will warrant us in assuming can be done-as a matter of fact, to-day 80,000 bushels are being hauled-but we will only assume it at 40,000, for the sake of argument, at $1.60 we have the following results : One train of 40,000 bushels at 12 cents per bushel will give $4,800. Assuming the train mileage to be 1,475-which are the figures given by the Minister of Finance, and not 1,400, as given by Mr. Blair-at $1.60 per train mile, you will have an expenditure of $2,360, or a profit on that individual train of $2,440. I may be wrong in my assumption, but the calculations are right. Assuming one train per day, or 300 per annum, of 40,000 bushels each, this would mean 12,000,000 bushels of wheat, or a profit of $732,000. Assuming that a train costs in winter from Winnipeg to St. John, a distance of 1,875 miles, $1.60 per train mile, you will have $3,000, according to the methods adopted by railways to get at the train mileage, while 40,000 bushels at a freight rate of 15 cents per bushel will represent $6,000, or a direct profit of $3,000 on the one train per day, or two in the winter time, of 40,000 bushels each, or 12,000,000 bushels in all, that will represent a profit of $900,000. Assuming that we could carry wheat in summer from Winnipeg to Quebec, say 12,000,000 bushels, we can make $732,000 if these figures be correct. And in winter time, we make $900,000. Or, on that wheat haulage alone, there will be a profit to the railway company of $1,632,000. Now, I am not relying altogether on my own estimate in this matter. I have submitted these figures to the railway authorities here at Ottawa, and they say that my premises, my reasoning and my deductions are correct. And I have not the slightest doubt that it is just upon such reasoning as that that the Grand Trunk authorities believed they could carry grain successfully from Winnipeg to Quebec and Sr. John, and compete, as they have a right to think they could, being endorsed in this matter by Sir Sandford Fleming, with the ;ail and water route. Now, the freight ( barges from Brandon to Montreal by lake and rail are 16-5 cents per bushel ; by lake and rail, with winter storage, 21-375 cents per bushel ; by rail direct to St. John, 21 885 cents per bushel. Against that competition this railway can successfully carry grain. To show that this calculation is incorrect you have first to show that an engine will not do on the Grand Trunk Paci-Mr. HEYD.
fie what it is doing on other railways, that a Canadian railway cannot be as economically run as another, or that on other railways under similar conditions, it costs more than $1.60 per train mile. If it costs $2 per train mile the profits would be correspondingly small.
Now, I give these figures for what they are worth. They certainly have made an impression on my mind. When I consider (he results I have brought forward together with the willingness of the Grand Trunk Railway Company-capable, careful business men, who know what a railway is capable of doing-I am satisfied I am not far out of the way.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) permit me to ask him a question ?
Why certainly.
Can the hon. gentleman understand why the government gave the excuse that the Grand Trunk must take this up or it would not go on, if there is such an immense fortune in this traffic?

The whole experience of (he American railways tells against the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd). Take, for instance, the transportation between Chicago and Buffalo. By rail the distance is only 510 miles ; by water it is nearly 900 miles. Yet, let my hon. friend look at the record of the grain trade and be will find that the lake carriers year by year have been taking nearly everything from the railways. Every argument that my hon. friend has deduced is contradicted by hard facts. Figures are strong, but facts are stronger, surely.

It is very singular, if all the facts contradict me, that so many bushels of wheat are hauled by the Grand Trunk from Midland and by the Canada Atlantic from Parry Sound in competition with this very water route.
By water and rail.

But it could be all by water. To the extent that it goes by rail, the fa ?t is demonstrated that it is cheaper to go by rail than to go by water, because it could go by all-water if there was any advantage in sending it that way. Yet, notwithstanding the competition, millions of bushels go over the Canada Atlantic, the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk in competition with the water route. The conditions under which these railways operate are not so favourable as those of the Grand Trunk Pacific will be. This road will be at Winnipeg itself. Our friends opposite always t: ke Fort William as the objective point, just as if grain from Edmonron. Prince Albert, Brandon or any of these other western towns and cities, could be carried for nothing to Fort William. Add the freight from any distant inland town in the Northwest

Territories to Fort William, to the cost of transportation by the water route to Montreal or Quebec, and you will see that the Grand Trunk Pacific could successfully compete. The Grand Trunk Pacific may get its load a thousand miles inland. To carry the load of 40,000 bushels over a railway of small gradients to Quebec would be almost as cheap as to carry it on an ordinary road to Fort William. For instance, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern have to carry grain nearly 600 miles over a low grade road before it reaches Fort William. The Grand Trunk Pacific carrying from Winnipeg to Quebec, -over a road of low gradients, would be half way to Quebec by the time the other had reached Fort William. You have to go into these facts much more carefully than my iion. friend has done, and not jump at such hasty conclusions. But it is said that the Grand Trunk has no motive in carrying their grain over the Grand Trunk Pacific. If it can be demonstrated that they can do it profitably, then we have the strongest guarantee that they will do it independent of the legal compulsions under the agreement. It is said that they prefer to build a railway from North Bay to Winnipeg, and, oast of North Bay to utilize their present system. What advantage would this be to the Grand Trunk Railway ? I can readily understand why they were willing to abandon their former scheme and take adi antage of their present one. The road is actually as short as theirs would have been, while it goes through a practically fertile territory, capable of evolving a large amount of local freight, while from Winnipeg to North Bay, under the conditions under which the Grand Trunk intended to build, the road for a thousand miles would hove been through a territory from which they would derive no freight. Now, take this Grand Trunk Pacific road from Winnipeg to the point about 175 miles north of North Bay, where it would be tapped by the Ontario government's railway. From Winnipeg to this junction point is about !;50 miles.
